speechtext: By leave of the house I should like to table a letter of thanks received from the President of the United States just before I left for the recent visit of parliamentarians to Washington. I think perhaps hon. members would like to hear the expression of appreciation.

maintopic: TABLING OF LETTER OF THANKS FROM PRESIDENT OF UNITED STATES
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TABLING OF LETTER OF THANKS FROM PRESIDENT OF UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The letter reads as follows: Dear Mr. Speaker:
The high point of my recent visit to Ottawa was the opportunity so generously accorded me to address the distinguished members of the Canadian parliament in the chamber of the House of Commons. Such an opportunity comes to few men and I am most grateful for it. I think the occasion was highly symbolic-and as such should be well noted throughout the world-of the splendid relationship enjoyed between your country and mine. In addition to registering my thanks for being invited to speak before parliament, I must add that I thoroughly enjoyed the experience.
Please accept my great appreciation for the very great consideration shown to my wife and myself during our visit to Ottawa. I note that you will be coming to Washington soon with other Canadian members of the United States-Canadian parliamentary group, and I hope to have the chance to thank you personally for your friendliness during my visit to Ottawa.
Sincerely,
John F. Kennedy.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES  ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING AIR DEFENCE AND PRODUCTION SHARING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some time representatives of the Canadian and United States governments have been working on an agreement relating to the defence of Canada, more particularly to air defence and to the Canada-United States production sharing program. The objective of such an agreement was to reflect the desire of both governments to ensure more effective use of the productive capacities, skills and resources of each country and at the same time to demonstrate our mutual determination to improve the defensive strength of NATO and particularly of NORAD under it.
An agreement has now been concluded which contains three major terms, all of which are closely interrelated.
(1)	By the terms of the Pine Tree line agreement of 1951, and a further agreement of 1955, responsibility for the Pine Tree line was divided between the two governments. Canada will assume responsibilities hitherto resting on the United States under these agreements for manning, operation, maintenance and financing 16 stations of this line. The take-over of these stations will begin immediately and will be carried out as fast as possible having regard to the R.C.A.F.'s capacity to assume these additional responsibilities, and will be so phased as to maintain the efficiency and effectiveness of the line.
(2)	In consideration of the financial and other benefits which will accrue to the United States as a result of Canada's assumption of additional responsibilities under the Pine Tree agreements, Canada will be furnished with 66 F-101B interceptor aircraft and appropriate support equipment. These aircraft, title to which will be vested in Canada, will be armed with conventional weapons and will serve to re-equip R.C.A.F. squadrons allocated to NORAD and will be operated in accordance with NORAD plans. As aircraft are already in existence, being the latest of that series off the production line, deliveries will commence immediately
6180	HOUSE OF
Canada-U.S. Air Defence Sharing and will be phased in accordance with the R.C.A.F.'s ability to absorb them.
The cost of spare parts, flight simulators and related equipment for these aircraft will be shared on the basis of the United States paying two thirds and Canada paying one third. The cost of the armament to be obtained for the aircraft will be shared on the same basis.
(3)	The United States agrees to the procurement in Canada of a number of F-104G aircraft, associated support equipment and initial spares to the total value of $200 million, of which the United States share will be $150 million and the Canadian share $50 million.
Mr. Speaker, I shall be asking leave at the conclusion of my remarks to table copies of the exchange of notes and the memorandum of understanding. So that the acting leader of the opposition and the acting leader of the C.C.F. party will have these notes and documents available now, I am sending them copies.
The aircraft procured will enable Canada and the United States to make a significant contribution to the collective strength of NATO under their respective mutual aid and defence assistance programs. The deliveries of these aircraft are to begin in mid-1963 following the completion of production of the aircraft of this type ordered for the first Canadian air division in Europe. It is anticipated that deliveries will be made at the approximate rate of 48 aircraft per year and will continue until the said sum of $200 million has been expended.
Mr. Speaker, this agreement, representing as it does an important and constructive development in Canada's defence relations with the United States, is futher evidence of the determination of both countries to maintain the operational effectiveness of the North American air defence system. It will make a significant contribution to the security of North America and to the European area of NATO as well.
I would stress that the approach of both governments has not been based on narrow self-interest but reflects a genuine effort to find a way for each to co-operate with the other, to the benefit not only of both but of mutual allies as well. The letter which we have just heard read from the President of the United States is the epitome of the relationship which is embodied in the agreement entered into.
The agreement is therefore more than just a bilateral agreement. It expresses the desire to make common use of those resources which each possesses and which can be made available for the benefit of each other and


our partners in NATO in the pursuit of peace, and makes possible a more substantial contribution toward the security of the west than could be made by either government acting alone.
Despite past indications and the widely accepted views of military staffs in the western world, and statements of Russian leaders too to the effect that the U.S.S.R. was completely replacing bomber aircraft with missiles, it has not done so and is continuing to maintain a large and effective fleet of bombers. Indeed, the experience of all the nations in the western world has been that widespread changes have had to be made in plans, and various armaments have had to be discarded as events have altered decisions previously made and as the U.S.S.R. has changed or has departed from anticipated courses of action.
The Canadian government has done much to support disarmament, but recent world events re-emphasize that the U.S.S.R. is obviously not of that mind. In the days ahead we shall continue the representations which have been made in the past. Indeed, the Secretary of State for External Affairs will leave tomorrow for Geneva. At the same time we must realize that there is no survival in adopting the attitude that if Canada does not maintain her most effective defences her people will thereby escape havoc and destruction should war come. Canada, in common with the other nations of the free world, must therefore continue to maintain its defences.
Now I ask leave to table the exchange of notes and the memorandum of understanding in both languages.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

Mr. Speaker, the announcement the Prime Minister has just made is an important one, and I am sure it will be welcomed by the country at large. The Prime Minister has divided his announcement into three parts. He has referred first to the assumption by Canada of the Pine Tree line and the 16 stations, in consideration for which Canada will get the 66 Voodoo fighters for certain purposes. Third, the United States agrees to procure from Canada 200 F-104G aircraft to the value of roughly $200 million.
In so far as the general purport of the Prime Minister's statement is concerned, I say at once that we on this side of the house welcome it. However, there are certain aspects on which I should like to comment briefly. I feel that so far as the F-101 jet fighter, the Voodoo, is concerned, we on this side are glad to see this replacement. We think it is a worth-while replacement; we should have this

aircraft in order to allow the R.C.A.F. to control and maintain sovereignty over Canadian skies.
In so far as the cost is concerned, that is another matter. If we add into the deal the cost of the operation and maintenance of the Pine Tree line, this amount will be but a down payment on the triangular deal.
In so far as the deal itself is concerned, I cannot refrain from making this comment; that if the government had put as much effort into selling the Avro Arrow, which was the most advanced interceptor in the western world, we might have been successful in achieving this agreement much earlier. It is unfortunate that the effort was put into selling the United States plane, even though it is extremely helpful that a substantial part will be purchased from Canadair of Montreal and the Orenda engines from Toronto and Malton as well. It seems to us if that had been done and much more effort had been put into trying to sell the Canadian plane, our research and development in Canada should not have suffered.
The original deal, sir, included, I believe, a triangular exchange of the CL-44, which is built by Canadair in Montreal, for the F-101. It seems to us on this side of the house that deal would have been more advantageous than the one which has been announced. We regret that because of this long procrastination on the part of the government it has taken now many, many months, running into several years-

Order. I do not wish to establish a new practice. In this house we have followed a course permitting the government to make factual statements in respect of policy or administrative action, as in this case, as well as allowing comment from the opposition without thereby entering into a debate. This practice is not easy to apply or to follow. When it is clear that a statement is for the information of this house and is presented here rather than having hon. members of this house receive the information elsewhere, the right of comment is very limited, and if the comment goes beyond that limitation or tends to enter into the realm of the making of assertions of a controversial character which no hon. member could expect to leave unchallenged, then the problem is presented that the government inevitably seeks the right to comment on that sort of statement.
It has not been the practice to permit the minister to reply. I have indicated that where, in the course of comments from the opposition a statement has been misinterpreted it is an inherent right of the minister as it would be of any member whose statement had been misinterpreted to seek to correct the misinterpretation by an explanation. But I would not like to see the practice develop, unless by consent of the house, of replying in kind to remarks which have been improperly permitted to go on the record. Therefore I trust that the hon. member for Laurier will not put the Prime Minister, who made the statement, in the position of having either to leave the accusation stand or ask to initiate a new practice.

I thank the Prime Minister for sending over this correspondence and memorandum of understanding. Of course he will understand that we have only a few minutes to glance at it. The announcement he has just made is very important, involved and complicated; therefore I am sure the house will understand that we shall require time to study it fully and appreciate all its implications. We shall take that time, Mr. Speaker, and deal with the matter fully on the defence estimates.

In view of the cancellation of the contract with the Avro people, a British firm, to their great cost and inconvenience, and in view of our present relations with Great Britain and concern over the common market and so on, I think this has broader implications than are confined just to this straight matter of the announcement and the issue at stake. Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce based on a statement reported to have been made by Hon. J. Wilfrid Spooner, minister of lands and forests of the province of Ontario. I wish to quote the statement because it causes some eyebrow raising, to say the least. The statement reads in part:
Canada needs more salesmen in Europe, lands and forests minister J. Wilfrid Spooner said yesterday following a tour of the United Kingdom, France, Switzerland, West Germany, the Soviet union, Sweden and Finland.
He said Canada's trade representatives should intensify their activities. In his view, these officials are highly qualified but are hampered by a shortage of staff and inadequate facilities.
Would the minister inform the house whether, in his opinion, his department has the number of trade representatives with adequate facilities necessary to satisfactorily promote the sale of Canadian products abroad?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY ONTARIO CABINET MEMBER
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his intention to ask the question. I have checked into the matter, and I understand that Mr. Spooner was referring to the commercial representatives of commercial companies which he felt were in greater need in the markets in which he had been travelling.
With regard to our own trade commissioners, permit me to say that we have 120 commissioners presently stationed abroad in 62 posts in 48 countries. Their offices are located in the principal commercial centres of the world. The record indicates that these men are well trained, enthusiastic and effective. The annual report of my department for the year 1960 records that their joint efforts influenced more than $100 million worth of new export business for Canada in that year.
May I also remind the house of the effective trade promotion work that these officers have carried out in consequence of the export trade promotion conference held in Ottawa last December. I regularly receive letters of commendation from Canadian businessmen who indicate that they are getting the trade promotional assistance from the trade commissioner service of which they stand in need.
The service recruits new officers annually. Seven young men are in the last weeks of

Inquiries of the Ministry their training now and will be going to their first posts by early autumn. Twelve new recruits are about to report for training. With these young men we will be able to strengthen posts which need additional officers; equally, we will be able to open new posts where this is warranted. In the last 18 months we have been able to open four new posts at Canberra, Moscow, Lagos and Philadelphia. I believe that the record of new business influences, the approbation of Canadian exporters, and the international reputation of the Canadian trade commissioner service indicate that it is meeting its responsibilities.
With regard to greater efforts being made abroad by the sales representatives of commercial firms in Canada, I agree with Mr. Spooner that there are tremendous additional sales opportunities for many of our products in the markets of the world. I believe that, and I have urged continually upon Canadian firms which produce goods for which there is a market abroad that they intensify their selling efforts in these potential markets.

There are many objectionable features to this bill which were brought to the attention of the minister during the sittings of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and I should like to deal with them now. They have to do with exemption from payment of pilotage dues of United States vessels moving in the pilotage district from Montreal to Cornwall-St. Regis, giving the United States vessels a privilege which they do not possess under the treaties signed between Canada and the United States over the years. There is the question of sovereignty involved in this matter, wherein I believe Canada is ceding to United States vessels sovereignty in purely Canadian waters, and there is also involved a question of safety in navigation.
In order to put the matter in perspective I think I should say there are seven groups of pilots established on the Seaway. There are four groups, totalling 200, whose territories cover purely Canadian waters. There are the groups in the Quebec district which involves an area from Quebec to tide water; in the Montreal district, which involves an area from Montreal to Quebec; in the harbour of Montreal; and fourth, in the Cornwall district, which is the pilotage district established last November by the Department of Transport and which extends from Montreal to Cornwall-St. Regis.
Then there are three other groups totalling 92 men whose territories cover international waters. They are the three districts known as
Canada Shipping Act
international pilotage districts: district No. 1, Cornwall to Kingston; district No. 2, Welland canal and waters connecting lakes Erie and Huron; and district No. 3, waters connecting lakes Huron and Superior.
Beginning May 1 of this year the so-called great lakes pilotage regulations which have been worked out over two years of negotiation between Canada and the United States, came into effect. I refer here to the act which was passed last year and which is known as chapter 40 of the Statutes of Canada 8 and 9 Elizabeth II, 1960, which established part VIa of the Canada Shipping Act and set up what is known as great lakes pilotage.
What is rather astounding to me is that this was done after an agreement had been entered into between the Minister of Transport acting on behalf of Canada and the secretary of commerce of the United States. This agreement was signed by the present Minister of Transport on May 1, 1961 and by the secretary of commerce of the United States on April 28, 1961. It is strange that in this agreement, which covers the whole field in the great lakes, no mention whatsoever is made of the exemption from payment of pilotage dues in the area from Montreal to Cornwall-St. Regis.
In order to bring the matter, as I think it should be brought, to the attention of the committee, it is necessary to point out that what is being sought here is this. Perhaps I should just put on the record again what is demanded by the government through the Department of Transport, namely that ships registered in Canada or the United States whose operations are upon the great lakes, or between ports in the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river, or whose operations are primarily as described in subparagraph 1 and which make occasional voyages to ports in the maritime provinces of Canada while operating in any pilotage district on the St. Lawrence river above the pilotage district of Montreal, shall be exempt from the payment of pilotage dues.
As was stated in the committee, this has the same meaning and effect as the exemption from compulsory pilotage. Therefore this means that United States ships travelling in the Montreal-Cornwall-St. Regis district will be exempt from the payment of pilotage dues. In other words, it will not be necessary for them to have a Canadian pilot on board. They may, if they wish, take one on, but there is no obligation so to do, and the masters and mates of those vessels may, if they so desire, take the ship right through.
I say, first of all, that this is an infringement upon the sovereign rights of Canada in these international waters. In so stating I should like to make brief reference to the

Canada Shipping Act
manner in which this whole subject was dealt with by treaty. I refer to the evidence given by Dr. Skelton, former deputy minister of external affairs, before a committee of the other place dealing with the development and improvement of the St. Lawrence river. This evidence can be found in the proceedings of a special committee of the other place in 1928. Dr. Skelton was giving evidence before that committee, and he dealt with the various treaties covering this matter. I refer to page 70 of those proceedings and I quote Dr. Skelton's words:
Coming then to the treaties dealing with the St. Lawrence, we begin, of course, with the treaty of 1783, ending the war of American independence. It was there provided, you will recall, that the boundary between the United States and Canada was to run along the 45th parallel-
That is the 45th parallel of latitude:
-until it struck the St. Lawrence and was to follow the middle of the river St. Lawrence up to lake Ontario.
There was some dispute about the line, which I need not go into now. Then Dr. Skelton went on:
Now, the next treaty point to which I need refer is the Ashburton-Webster treaty of 1842 ... Article 7 of the Ashburton-Webster treaty reads as follows:
"It is further agreed, that the channels in the river St. Lawrence on both sides of the Long Sault islands and of Barnhart island, the channels in the river Detroit, on both sides of the island Bois Blanc, and between that island and both the Canadian and American shores, and all the several channels and passages between the various islands lying near the junction of the river St. Clair with the lake of that name, shall be equally free and open to the ships, vessels and boats of both parties."
Dr. Skelton went on to deal with the treaty of Washington which was passed in 1871, article 26 of which reads as follows:
The navigation of the river St. Lawrence, ascending and descending from the 45th parallel of north latitude, where it ceases to form the boundary between the two countries, from, to, and into the sea, shall forever remain free and open for the purposes of commerce to the citizens of the United States, subject to any laws and regulations of Great Britain or of the dominion of Canada, not inconsistent with such privilege of free navigation.
Then Dr. Skelton said:
That is from Cornwall to St. Regis. The second paragraph of the same article provides:
I will not read it because it deals with rivers other than the St. Lawrence. Until the treaty of 1871 there was never any question of conferring on United States citizens any rights below the Cornwall-St. Regis line. Then we come to the boundary waters treaty of 1909, the preliminary article of which reads as follows:
For the purposes of this treaty boundary waters are defined as the waters from main shore to main shore of the lakes and rivers and connecting waterways, or the portions thereof, along which the international boundary between the United States and the Dominion of Canada passes, including all

bays, arms and inlets thereof, but not including tributary waters which in their natural channels would flow into such lakes, rivers and waterways, or waters flowing from such lakes, rivers, and waterways, or the waters of rivers flowing across the boundary.
Then Dr. Skelton added this significant statement:
Now, there may be boundary waters to which article 1 specifically applies. Boundary waters roughly include part of the St. John river, the Ste. Croix river, the St. Lawrence river from Cornwall to lake Ontario-
That is above, but not below. He was asked this significant question by Hon. Mr. Reid:
But would not include from Cornwall to the sea?
Dr. Skelton: It would not, senator.
So I say all the rights which have been given by treaty to United States vessels and United States citizens have to do with international sections of the river, that is from the Cornwall-St. Regis line, the international boundary line, up to the head of the great lakes; but the area from the Cornwall-St. Regis line down to the gulf has been considered through the years to be purely Canadian waters.
What is being done here is to enact a bill by way of an amendment to a section which has the effect of a treaty giving rights to United States vessels which they do not possess today. What we are doing, sir, is abandoning to the United States our right to insist that their ships be piloted by Canadian pilots in an important and costly section of the St. Lawrence river. Furthermore, we are abandoning our right to determine the qualifications necessary for such pilots in this section of the river. We thereby concede to the United States a status equal to that of the owners and operators of our own vessels. We therefore lose our legitimate right of control of navigation in these waters, and we do all this without treaty. There is therefore no give and take.
The minister stated during the sittings of the committee that as far as he was concerned nothing would be done below Montreal, and we replied that we think this is a step in that direction. It is all right for the minister to give his assurance that this will not be done, and I am sure that in making that statement the minister was sincere. However, we know that conditions change, that circumstances alter, and a minister may move from one department to another. A statement such as that has no value with respect to legislation; it has no effect and no legislative force at all.
There is therefore being enacted here legislation which we fear will be a step toward exempting the other districts from the payment of pilotage dues. What is very difficult

to understand is why Canadian ships should be included in this when they are exempt already by an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act. The committee will probably have realized that under one of the sections of the Canada Shipping Act, namely section 346 (e), steamships registered in any part of Her Majesty's dominions are exempt from the payment of pilotage dues. It is difficult to understand why we should create a redundancy by including them in this bill.
There is also the question of safety of navigation. I think it should be brought to the attention of the committee that the waters from the Cornwall-St. Regis area down to Montreal are dangerous waters; they are considered as treacherous in some areas. In fact I believe the water drops close to 100 feet from that point down to the port of Montreal. Very costly navigation facilities have been constructed in this area. There are the St. Lambert lock and the Ste. Catherine lock on the south shore, the two locks at Beauharnois, the channels between these locations and the stretch from the upper Beauharnois to the international boundary line. Why the government has seen fit to exempt this area and put it in the same class as the international pilotage area is difficult to understand, particularly when last year it introduced legislation in this house which covered those international waters in the great lakes area. It seems that after this was done negotiations were entered into between Canada and the United States, in which Canada probably gave the United States to understand that it would grant this exemption in a purely Canadian section of the river.
It has been clearly stated in the committee that this is a serious infringement of the rights of the pilots, let alone the sovereign rights of Canada. In any event, from the point of view of safety there is also the consideration that pilots who normally operate for six to eight hours will, because of this, have to work longer hours. Hence it seems to those of us who sit on this side that there is an injustice being done to the Canadian pilots.
I shall not repeat here what was said by Mr. Lalonde appearing on behalf of the pilots and by Mr. Langlois appearing on behalf of the guild, but it is worth while to remind the minister of the definitions which were given in the former act, chapter 40, referred to earlier, where the great lakes pilotage area was described. It is clear that the description ends at the Cornwall-St. Regis dividing line.
Then the minister indicated, in the committee, I believe, that the Cornwall-Montreal district would remain as it is, and that ships whose captains were desirous of taking on pilots could do so. This would mean that the
Canada Shipping Act
Canadian government would have to maintain a pool of pilots, presumably, in the Cornwall area at the city of Cornwall; because if United States vessels are going to have the option of taking on pilots, pilots must be provided and a pool established. I presume the logical place for that would be the city of Cornwall. However, there would be no obligation upon the captains of United States vessels to use these pilots, and they might well decide to sail right through without using the services of the pilots.
The objection we see to the part of the bill with which I am now dealing is twofold. First, it is giving to United States vessels rights which they do not now possess by treaty. All the rights and privileges of United States citizens in the international waters of the St. Lawrence have heretofore been granted by treaty, and it is difficult to understand why in a section which is purely Canadian an attempt is being made to give an exemption which does not exist in the rest of the waters of the St. Lawrence. The next point to which we draw attention is the fact that in this area the waters are swift and treacherous. We object to the provision now being made. We think it should be made compulsory to take on pilots, and that this exemption should not be granted.
These are the remarks which I have intended to make, and I hope they will be received by the minister in the manner in which I feel they should.

I wish to direct my remarks to the point which has been covered by the hon. member for Laurier. We cannot take a narrow or parochial view of this amendment. The St. Lawrence seaway is one, from Fort William and Port Arthur in the west to Montreal in the east, and from the United States ports of Duluth and Chicago in the American west to Montreal in the east. There is no practical possibility of devising an artificial boundary or terminal for the seaway at Cornwall or St. Regis. The economic end of the seaway is Montreal, and that, too, is where the United States contribution to the works of the seaway stopped.
We have heard the hon. member for Laurier demand on many occasions that an economic survey of the effect of the seaway be made. I represent a riding on Georgian bay, part of the great lakes system which was probably more affected in its economic life by the seaway than any other part. Many of us, and many other people interested in shipping, wish that the survey which the hon. member now requests had been made when he was in a position of administrative responsibility and could have had it carried out himself.

Canada Shipping Act
In order to straighten out a few of the facts I think a timetable of the negotiations which preceded this amendment might be useful to the committee. We shall begin in the summer of 1960, a year ago. Negotiations for the joint pilotage of all the confined waters of the seaway between ourselves and the United States began in September, 1960. The pilots between Kingston and Montreal made certain demands on the government-we should be clear as to this-prior to November, 1960. There was no compulsory pilotage, nor was there compulsory payment of pilotage dues between Kingston and Montreal in either section of that area.
In September, 1960, the pilots in that area made certain demands or requests of the Minister of Transport. As a result of these requests the area from Kingston to Montreal was made a compulsory pilotage dues area.
1 think the exact date was November 17, 1960. At that time the pilots were told that United States shipping would likely be exempted in this particular section. The pilots told us in "the committee that they did not agree, and I can understand that they did not agree. However, they were certainly warned in November, 1960 of what was going to happen.
Following the order in council and the negotiations, a press release was issued by the pilots in Montreal. The United States representatives negotiating the agreement took up this press release and brought it to the attention of representatives of the Department of Transport who were negotiating with them. They said that if we wanted to get an over-all agreement with the United States we would have to exempt United States vessels from the payment of compulsory pilotage dues in this area, St. Regis to Montreal. I think that is an understandable demand on the part of the United States. After all, it has contributed many millions of dollars to the improvement of the seaway works in that particular area of the seaway.
I should like to again emphasize the fact that Montreal is the eastern terminal of the seaway. Much has been made of the fact that this particular area was not included in the agreement, nor in the definition of the great lakes basin. As I understand it, the reason for that is quite clear. The area from St. Regis to Montreal involves only Canadian waters, just as the waters of lake Michigan are completely United States waters and are not covered by the agreement. However, the United States has exempted our ships from compulsory pilotage regulations in respect of the waters of lake Michigan.
As a final note regarding the sequence of events which preceded this amendment, I should like to say that agreement with the

United States in respect of pilotage was concluded in May of this year, and provides equal pilotage rates in those sections of the waters which are bordered by the two countries.
A great deal has been said during this debate regarding sovereignty. It has been suggested that if we give up something by treaty we give up some of our sovereignty, because in order to recover that which we had lost a breach of that treaty would be incurred. I suggest we have not given up any of our sovereignty in this way because in respect of Canadian waters we have done this by act of parliament rather than by treaty. Surely there is no derogation of our sovereignty in the passing of a law which can be repealed by a future parliament. 1 suggested this involves much less in the way of derogation of our Canadian sovereignty than would be involved had it been done by treaty.
In regard to this subject, the hon. member for Laurier has suggested that we have established a precedent and that the United States will be asking next for free pilotage from Montreal to the open waters at the mouth of the St. Lawrence river. I suggest we have not established a precedent of that kind at all. The United States has contributed nothing to the building of the seaway works beyond Montreal and has no right to do so. However, we are dealing with portions of the St. Lawrence seaway development above St. Regis, toward which the United States has directed millions of dollars.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Did I understand him to say that the United States is spending millions of dollars toward this development?
I said "has", using the past tense.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The United States has not spent one cent toward the development of this section of the seaway. Surely my hon. friend should know that.
They did not?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The United States has spent money in the section from Cornwall to St. Regis upstream, not downstream.

That is what I said. The hon. member misunderstood me, or perhaps I did not make myself sufficiently clear.
Regarding the question of sovereignty, it seems to me that one obvious area where we may have lost sovereignty resulted from the location of the eastern end of the western part of the works entering lake Ontario. It might very well have been located in the channel north of Wolfe island, and would

then have been entirely in Canadian waters, rather than south of Wolf island so that it is more logical to locate our pilot stations on the United States side.
I suggest that the issue in respect of safety is not a clear issue at all. The available statistics do not clearly establish the value of pilotage. A great many people fall into the common error of thinking that because a ship had an accident when there was not a pilot aboard, the accident occurred because of that fact. Surely that cannot be a valid understanding, because the corollary would be that if a pilot was aboard at a time the ship had an accident, regardless of the reason, the responsibility would be entirely his. In this regard I suggest that the department should keep statistics in such fashion as to indicate clearly whether these accidents resulted because of the fact that a pilot was or was not aboard.
It is true that these confined areas of the seaway are hazardous. However, I suggest the hazards are much less than before as a result of the great changes which have been made in recent years. Many Canadian captains as well as United States captains have had much experience in operating through the seaway. I suggest those captains have had much more experience in this regard than the captains of ocean going vessels. It must be remembered that great lakes masters, whether Canadian or American, because of their activities have much more experience in handling ships along this seaway than captains of sea-going vessels who are more interested in navigation. For that reason there are many more competent pilots among our Canadian and American masters than among the masters of those sea-going vessels. While much larger ships, such as the 735-foot bulk carriers, are now using the seaway, it must be remembered that those ships are equipped with many safety devices and are handled with greater ease than many of the older ships. I suggest the matter of safety, for that reason, is again inconclusive. I also suggest that if safety is a prime requirement, then compulsory pilotage is the answer.
It has been equated that the imposition of pilotage dues in effect makes pilotage compulsory. In the final analysis of the situation I suggest that is not true at all. However, if safety is a prime consideration there ought to be compulsory pilotage. In this regard, pilots have stated that the imposition of compulsory pilotage will not affect their earnings, and that they have been given the assurance it will not. We have been informed by pilots appearing before the standing committee that prior to November of 1960, when there were no restrictions at all, no ship, either Canadian or United States,
Canada Shipping Act
attempted to go through this section of the seaway without a pilot. I suggest it will be some considerable time before any will make such an attempt.
When considering the effect of this amendment on the operation of the whole seaway and the great lakes system, I suggest it is a good one. Many bogeys have been raised which on examination are found to be invalid, and I do not think we should be embarrassed because of this amendment being made after our agreement with the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Laurier raised many points this morning which had been raised earlier during our consideration in the committee, as well as during meetings of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I feel that many of his questions have been extremely well answered by the hon. member for Simcoe North, and that he has dealt with the most important of them. However, I feel it is my duty as minister to bring forward certain suggestions for the consideration of this committee so as to clarify the situation so there will be no misunderstanding regarding the policy of the government.
We are very fortunate in Canada in having extremely well qualified pilots. They are parts of very old corporations; they have ancient traditions. I should not like to leave the impression that we are in any way putting a strain on the very good relations that the Department of Transport, my officials and myself have always had with the members of the pilotage trade. However, I think I should take this opportunity to make sure that the committee has the actual facts as events happened prior to the decision of the government to bring forth this amendment.
As the hon. member for Simcoe North explained, there was a certain difficulty with the pilots last November. We had some very long sessions with them in which we discussed the general policy of the department on the matter of pilotage on the St. Lawrence, and also more particularly the formation of a new district for the Kingston-Cornwall-Montreal area. At that time the pilots made quite a point of this. They requested from the department, myself and the shipping authorities in Canada the imposition of compulsory dues for all ships except Canadian ships going from Cornwall to Montreal and from Montreal to Cornwall.
Well, that would have been quite a step, because by this move we would have recognized a new pilotage district, and we would be imposing compulsory dues in a pilotage district for the first time. Prior to that time all ships in that particular district had been

Canada Shipping Act
exempt, Canadian ships, commonwealth ships, British ships, foreign ships and United States ships. We wanted the pilots in that area to be put in the same position as other pilots on the St. Lawrence. We conceded that, but I remember very well-and I was the spokesman for the government-that I told the pilots myself that we were going to impose compulsory dues but at the first opportunity we would exempt United States ships by law, by an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act, because in all fairness we thought it would have been unfair and unnecessary to impose compulsory dues on United States ships.
The pilots themselves recognized the soundness of my argument. At that time, in November, I said to them, "Well, so that we do not upset the apple cart, and owing to the fact that it is pretty late in the season and we cannot have an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act except very late in the next session, will you exempt the Americans yourselves?" I simply said, "Is it satisfactory to you that as far as United States ships are concerned, you agree not to charge them anything until the end of the year?" The pilots, who were extremely pleased to see that we were imposing compulsory dues on foreign ships apart from United States ships, were agreeable to that. They agreed not to impose dues on United States ships. I remember very well they also said, "Of course we are not in favour of the exemption of any ships, so we will probably have to put in a sort of objection to that but it will be pro forma." That is pretty well the situation.
The hon. member for Laurier talked about sovereignty. I should like to remind the committee that there is absolutely nothing in this amendment to the shipping act which says that a United States pilot will do any pilotage in any Canadian waters. Of course, if any ship requires a pilot from the Canadian border and from St. Regis-Cornwall to Montreal and lower down the river, the law is there, the shipping act is there always to make sure that the pilot will be a Canadian. The only thing we are doing is exempting the Americans as we exempt commonwealth ships in those areas.
As far as safety is concerned, I think it is even more important and more logical to exempt United States ships than commonwealth ships for this reason. The United States ships are lakers and, of course, the United States laker captains have had experience in these waters; they have been plying in these waters all their lives and are in a much better position to man their own ships than others. They know exactly how their ships react in various currents, winds,

and so forth. United States captains are certainly more qualified than the captains of commonwealth or British ships who come in those waters only once or twice a season.
So far as the safety factor is concerned, my hon. friend from Simcoe North puts forward a very good argument when he says that the new seaway, with better aids to navigation, better lighthouses, wider canals and so forth, is certainly a safer area for ships than it was before. My hon. friend from Laurier will admit the inference that it should be safer for a ship to go through those waters than it was before. Of course the traffic may be heavier than it was before, but I do not think the fact that we have this seaway has increased the danger; on the contrary, I think it has decreased the danger in those waters.
I think this is about all I have to say at the present time, but I want to repeat that in what we are doing there is nothing extraordinary at all. United States ships have never paid any dues in those waters. The only reason they were included in the act, and that we must have a special amendment, is that it was too late last November to exempt them by legislation. We told the pilots at that time -they agreed among themselves and they were extremely pleased to see it-that we were imposing compulsory dues on foreign vessels.
I think it is a good thing to have compulsory dues on foreign vessels, because it pretty well forces them to take on pilots. Foreign ships are a real danger in these waters, because their officers and crews have not the experience and they are really the ones who can cause damage. I think safe navigation in the seaway, our relations with our United States friends, and the guarantee of progressive shipping operations in this area all will be secured by this amendment to the act. Therefore I strongly recommend to the committee the adoption of clause 15.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Some statements have been made both by the hon. member for Simcoe North and by the minister which should be discussed at greater length, if not challenged entirely. The hon. member for Simcoe North regretted that a parochial view was being taken of this matter. I am sure the hon. member does not understand the situation, otherwise he would not have used that expression. Surely the pilots who operate in the whole of the seaway are not taking a parochial view, and they have opposed this legislation. They have not opposed it because of a parochial attitude; they have opposed it because they think these are matters which have been disposed of in the past by treaty, and which should not be regulated by amendment to the Canada Shipping Act in this fashion.

Then the Canadian Labour Congress has put itself on record as being opposed to this amendment, and has given reasons for that opposition. I will not take the time of the committee to put on Hansard the telegram which was sent by the Canadian Labour Congress, but for those who want to read it I may say it can be found on page 173 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence, No. 6, of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. The labour congress certainly did not think they were taking a parochial view when they were dealing with this matter.
The hon. member for Simcoe North was inaccurate in a number of the statements he made. I am sure he will not feel that I want to be disrespectful to him in any way, because I want to deal with the matter as objectively as I can. In the first place, he said that the hon. member for Laurier had been advocating an economic survey of the seaway for a long time, and that if that had been done when that hon. member was in office, perhaps we would have better information available to us now. I have advocated such a survey for years now since I have been in this house, and I have given the reasons why it was not done when I was the president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. It was not done then because our job was to build the facilities for the seaway and not to seek the establishment of an economic survey, although I had asked certain economists to begin the work because I thought it would be a good thing for Canada, and they had embarked upon it but had not completed it. It was for this reason that I made recommendations to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines some years ago, and that recommendation was adopted but not a thing was done.
It seems strange to me, and I bring this to the attention of the hon. member for Simcoe North, that when the hon. member for Laurier suggests a matter which is approved unanimously, the government does not move. However, when it is some other member who suggests that, for instance, the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways be increased from seven to 12, the government accepts the suggestion right away with hardly any discussion in the committee. I shall leave it to the committee and to the hon. member for Simcoe North to decide for themselves whether political considerations motivate the government. However, let it be known to this committee that a recommendation for an economic survey was passed unanimously. It should have been acted upon, because it would have been a good thing for all these sections of the seaway today if that survey had been made.
Canada Shipping Act
Now, the hon. member for Simcoe North seems to be under a misapprehension as to the extent to which United States funds have been used in the construction of this section of the seaway. There was absolutely no United States money spent in the area of Cornwall-St. Regis and down to Montreal. Canadian funds only were used to construct the facilities, which were entirely in Canadian territory.
Then there was some question, both by the minister and by the hon. member for Simcoe North, of the seaway beginning at Montreal and going up to the head of the lakes. It was stated that it was logical, therefore, to exempt the pilots in this area. Well, I ask the minister and the hon. member, what is the definition of the seaway? According to one of the treaties between our two countries signed in the early days, the seaway begins below Quebec and goes up to the head of the lakes. Certainly in the report of an investigation made by engineers of Canada and the United States into the possibility of joint power and navigation development, the seaway is described as extending from below Quebec right up to the head of the lakes.
This is the fear of the pilots, that once you make any exemption for this fifth pilotage district, Montreal, Cornwall and St. Regis, the next step might very well be Montreal and Quebec, including Les Escoumains or down to Havre St. Pierre or wherever the new dividing line is likely to be. The objection raised by the pilots is that in the pilotage section of the Canada Shipping Act, which was enacted last year, you have already defined what you understand by the district to which this will apply. Certainly it ends at the international line, Cornwall-St. Regis. All the assurances and saving statements made by the minister, as the minister knows, from a legislative standpoint have no value whatever. There is no assurance that another step might not be taken at a later time.
Then the question of safety came up, and it was raised by both the minister and the hon. member. Safety is a prime consideration, but I ask this question. Who is to determine whether or not this is a safe pilotage area? I think the pilots certainly have as much experience of it as the officers of the department, if not far more. I say this with respect, because I have the greatest confidence in the officers of the Department of Transport.
I believe the minister was in error when he made a statement to the effect that United States vessels have been plying these waters all the time. This is not a fact, because I know the area. The United States vessels that have gone through these waters have used Canadian pilots, and that is why Canadian pilots have been stationed at Cornwall for

Canada Shipping Act
years and years. I could name many ot them. I can think now of Captain Ouellette, who plied from Prescott down to Montreal the greater part of his life. I knew him when I was a child, and people used to marvel at the way he would take a ship through the rapids down to Montreal. I can think of Mike Corkey, captain on the C.S.L. boats, who resided there many years. There were many masters. The United States vessels did not use their own captains. Few of them went through the old 14-foot canal system.
It is not accurate or correct to say, as has been stated here, that new aids to navigation have been established. This is not so. The aids to navigation extending from Cornwall-St. Regis to the international boundary line and down to the entrance to the new Beau-harnois canal are, for the most part, exactly the same as they were in the old canal. It is true that the canal is much deeper. It is true that the canal has been widened, and while it is the intention to modernize the aids to navigation they are still, for the most part, exactly the same as they were in the old canal system.
Here is the position. Whereas you had smaller ships carrying loads of 2,000 tons and having a draft of 12 to 14 feet operating in the old canal, now you have ships of 725 or 750 feet in length carrying loads of 25,000 tons which require greater care on the part of those who are operating them than ever before. Once you get into the canal, as was said by the hon. member for Simcoe North, it may well be that because of more modern equipment found on these ships you can manoeuvre through the canals at any rate more easily than was possible previously. But that does not apply to all the ships. There is still a large number of ships that are of the 14-foot calibre. I think the traffic report of the St. Lawrence seaway authority indicates that at least 25 per cent of the ships which moved up and down the seaway in the season of 1960 were of that variety.
The number is less and less every year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is quite true. In time, of course, vessels with draft under 25 feet will disappear entirely. How long it will take I do not know. According to the experts it may well be 10 years or more. I remember having heard an expert say it would take 25 years-this was before the seaway was built -before the 25-foot vessels would disappear entirely. As I say, last year about 25 per cent of the traffic was carried by these small vessels. As time goes on they will disappear; none the less it is not so much with regard to the small ships as with regard to the larger ships that one must be careful.

We had one sad experience I mentioned in committee; that of a United States pilot or captain, I have forgotten which, taking a ship through these dangerous waters, finding himself in serious difficulty, and blocking the passage for a substantial length of time. I therefore do not think it is fair or accurate to say that the safety of navigation will not be affected by this measure. I believe it will be affected, and the pilots say it will be affected. Surely those who have had experience all the way up and down this great river and these lakes should be given greater consideration than they have been given in this legislation.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

Under the agreement with the United States for the construction of a seaway was it not a condition that Canada make certain expenditures in the area from St. Regis to Montreal in addition to what the Americans were spending on the other sections in Montreal?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The only agreement there was between Canada and the United States is contained in the legislation which was passed by congress and the House of Commons, and in it there is no mention of that matter. I do not know what my hon. friend has in mind, but there certainly was no agreement as to the expenditure. There was United States legislation directing the United States corporation to build all the navigational facilities on the United States side of the line at a cost of $105 million, I think it was then, and there was Canadian legislation directing our authority either to build in Canada or to enter into an agreement with the United States for an understanding as to construction in the international section.
Finally what was arrived at was this. The United States decided to build a canal and two locks at Barnhart island on the United States side, and we decided to build a canal and one lock at Iroquois, Ontario, opposite Rockway Point, New York, but there was never any agreement as to the division of costs. The United States decided to build those facilities at a cost of $105 million then; I think they finally cost somewhat more than that. Our costs also increased over the estimate announced in those years.
I was just about to conclude by saying that I do not want to make this a contentious matter. I want to deal with it as objectively as possible. That is what I have tried to do this morning, as well as in the committee. However, I think it is a serious thing, first,

to deal in an act of parliament such as this, with a matter which has always been dealt with by treaty; and second, not to give greater consideration to the safety aspect in that part of the St. Lawrence which it seems to me is one of dangerous waters.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I also want to deal with this matter objectively, and I just want to answer shortly two or three points that have been raised by the hon. member for Laurier. The hon. member said that one of the big worries of the pilots is that this is a kind of first encroachment, and that it might have a tendency to produce the result of United States ships asking for exemption in the pilotage districts below Montreal. Mr. Chairman, United States ships have been exempt at all times right up to last November, and it has not produced any real pressure or nothing has been done with regard to exempting them from pilotage dues below Montreal. What we are doing at the present time actually is leaving the status quo as far as the United States is concerned. My hon. friend said that the ships are now larger and so on. I want to repeat that what we are doing is nothing new. United States ships have always been exempted. Of course many of them use pilots, and they are using pilots at the present time. However, when they do so they use Canadian pilots.
The hon. member for Laurier said I was making a comparison, as far as safety is concerned, between the pilots and the United States captains. That is not what I had in mind. As far as safety is concerned, what I am saying is that I do not think it is logical to exempt commonwealth ships and British ships, when their captains certainly cannot have had the same experience in these canals, these lakes and these waters as a United States laker captain who has been working all his life on ships plying these waters, although maybe not as a captain. I know of a United States captain who is in charge of a big laker and who has spent practically all of his life in lake waters. He therefore has had tremendous experience in these waters. When you are discussing safety, I think it would be illogical to allow a commonwealth ship to go up without being forced to take on a pilot and to refuse the same thing to the United States ships. I am also told that at the present time United States ships are using pilots and that they are Canadian pilots. We felt that this is a matter that should be left to them. They may develop some captains who are extremely used to these waters, and in some circumstances they might not feel that they need a pilot for one reason or another.
Canada Shipping Act
The other point raised by my hon. friend as far as safety is concerned is that we should not exempt United States ships because the situation is not the same at the present time; that ships are getting bigger and so on. May I say that the situation is exactly the same for Canadian ships. These huge long lakers going from lake Ontario to Montreal at the present time are new. They started on this route since the seaway was built. Our Canadian captains on our Canadian ships are faced with the same problem as that faced by United States captains on United States ships. There is no question of not exempting Canadian ships. So far as safety is concerned, I think we must not exaggerate this point. I am quite sure that the captain of a huge laker, when taking his ship down these waters and through these canals, will continue to take on our very good Canadian pilots if he is in any doubt about the safety of his ship.

On clause 9.

Mr. Chairman, this is a clause in this very important bill that we from British Columbia would certainly like the minister to comment upon. Coming from the west coast of British Columbia I must say that I was quite amazed to see one of the changes being made to this section. I can assure hon. members that it is of serious import to marine employees in British Columbia; they are very, very much concerned about its application.
I realize that a brief may have been presented to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines by Mr. R. G. Greaves, president of the national association of marine engineers of Canada, but as I am not a member of that standing committee I do not know just what consideration was given to this section or what consideration has been given by the minister to the brief on behalf of this association.

Canada Shipping Act
I do want to emphasize the seriousness with which clause 9	(2) (1) (iii) is viewed in
British Columbia, in particular by all tug boat employees. Very briefly I should like to point out that this particular phase of the clause makes a major change with regard to whether or not there is to be an engineer continuously on duty on tug boats having a certain nominal horsepower.
I am not going to go very deeply into this question of nominal horsepower, because it is something which I have not been able to fully understand. If it is electrical horsepower, I know it; if it is brake horsepower, I know it; but nominal horsepower is something rather nebulous. I understand these words were used at the end of the last century, although the expression was not included in our own act until 25 or 26 years ago. Nominal horsepower, as I have been able to understand it, is horsepower which is based on the area of a piston, but it does not have any relationship whatsoever in these modern times, to the stroke or the speed of the piston. Therefore nominal horsepower actually, in this day and age, does not bear any relationship to brake horsepower.
However, if my information is correct the majority of tug boats in British Columbia are going to be most seriously affected by a change being made to section 9, in that it will enable tug boat owners to comply with the act and will yet result, according to the national association of marine engineers, in a lay-off of between 50 and 100 engineers.
There is not only the factor of the laying-off of between 50 and 100 engineers who are employed on tug boats off the coast of British Columbia to be considered. There is also the most important question of safety.
I just cannot understand how this recommendation could come from anybody who knows the coast line of British Columbia. We have literally hundreds of dangerous channels. During particular periods of the year we have very, very severe rain and fog conditions. In addition, there has been a radical change in the tug boat industry, not only with regard to the greater power and efficiency of the motors themselves but also in their speed and in the loads they tow. It is not so long ago that the large log booms were towed at approximately one and one half to two knots per hour, but now we have the new log barges carrying between 3,000 and 4,000 tons of logs being towed at between seven and eight knots per hour.
In view of the increased power-that is, the brake horsepower-in tug boats today, this matter of safety is mighty important. Many of these tug boats have been re-engined in the last two or three years.
