speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

When the committee adjourned at one o'clock I was discussing a certain phase of clause 9 which is of serious import to those engaged on coastal work in tow boats in British Columbia, and which seriously concerns that industry as far as the safety of its employees is concerned.
In the few minutes during which I spoke I made mention of the fact that in this clause we still have the legislation aligned with an antiquated term, namely "nominal horsepower". I made some mention of that, and I pointed out the difference between nominal horsepower and brake horsepower. I should like to return to this question of nominal horsepower and relate it to the point I had taken up at one o'clock, namely the safety of tow boat operations in British Columbia.
I do not think the advance made in the efficiency and power of the engines used in tow boats has generally been recognized. I am advised, and it was confirmed by my reading during the lunch hour, that the actual change in the relation between nominal horsepower and brake horsepower has been fantastic. I have discovered that an engine as fitted to a tow boat in 1935, a four cylinder diesel engine with a nominal horsepower rating of just over 10, was capable of developing 240 brake horsepower. Today a modern engine such as the Werkespor diesel of four cylinders, rated at 8.6 nominal horsepower, is capable of developing 800 brake horsepower. Thus a modem engine whose nominal horsepower is rated at less than an engine turned out in 1935 can develop 800 brake horsepower as compared with 240 horsepower, and the remarkable increase in the power of modem tow boats at once becomes apparent. Yet because of an insistence for some reason or another in clause 9 that the power of a propelling engine should be measured in terms of nominal horsepower, proper consideration is not given to the work of the engineers, the responsibility of the engineers, and the increasing necessity for paying attention to safety.
It is my understanding that at the present time in British Columbia there are approximately 160 tow boats which require two engineers or, as I believe the proper term has

it, a continuous watch. If this provision of clause 9 which I am now discussing comes into effect it is my understanding that not more than 30 tow boats on the British Columbia coast will require a continuous watch involving two engineers. Irrespective of the increased efficiency and brake horsepower of diesel motors on tow boats, one of the basic reasons for the practical development of this greater power lies in automation, or the automatic control of these engines. The majority of those instruments and gauges operate on electricity. I should like all hon. members to realize that fact. I am aware of the situation, as I am an electrician by trade although perhaps a member of parliament by profession. I appreciate what can happen to automatic electrical equipment as the result of salt brine in the air and oily conditions in engine rooms, as well as because of disturbances through the vibrations caused by choppy water. Many of the new engines have automatic electrical gauges which require close examination and attention to make sure they are working properly. The checking of these instruments must be done by highly skilled individuals who understand their workings.
With the adoption of clause 9 of this bill between 50 and 100 engineers are going to be employed on a 12 hours on and 12 hours oft basis in British Columbia. This will have the result that an engineer will be in the engine room for a 12 hours period, and during his 12 hours oft duty the deckhand, the master or the mate will have to check the gauges. How will an inexperienced deckhand, or even a master or mate, be able to tell at a glance what is happening in the engine room below? I suggest they will not know because they are not trained to tell whether these highly automatic and delicate instruments are working properly.
That is my first point regarding safety. My second point has to do with the greatly increased efficiency and power of these engines which, as I pointed out earlier, on some occasions enable tow boats to travel from one and a half knots per hour to approximately eight knots per hour in British Columbia waters. I suggest the dangers involved are terrific. If this clause, particularly that portion regarding the nominal horsepower ratings is adopted, a situation will develop where the vast majority of tow boats operating off British Columbia will do so without engineers being on duty for at least 50 per cent of the time. Surely it cannot be expected that masters, mates or deckhands of these tow boats, who have other responsibilities, will know what these gauges and instruments indicate, particularly when their duties keep them in other parts of the ship than the engine room.
Canada Shipping Act
I should like to point out that the coast line of British Columbia is very tricky and dangerous from the point of navigation. I have had the privilege of living on the British Columbia coast for some 50 years. I have travelled along the coast on innumerable occasions from the Fraser river on the south to the Nass river on the north, by C.P.R. and C.N.R. steamship and by Union Steamship as well as by fishing boat, and know the situation which exists there. There are hundreds upon hundreds of passengers carried along this coast, to say nothing of the passengers carried on the inland waters which are plied mainly by tow boats twisting and turning up the river.
I do not intend to be derogatory to British Columbia in any way when I say there is quite a bit of fog, rain and stormy weather there, but that is the fact. As a result of this situation the masters and mates of these vessels must focus their attention, particularly during storms, on the navigation aspect rather than the operation of the engine. I think it is well known that in past years these masters have depended on echo sound to know where they were in these channels. They did this by blowing their whistle and counting the seconds until the echo was heard. In order to do this successfully one must give careful concentration. I understand that many ships today are equipped with radar, but even with that equipment the master and mate must direct their attention to those instruments and not the instruments in the wheel house which show the condition of the engine. However, the adoption of this clause will mean that the masters and mates, and in certain cases even the deckhands, will have to divide their attention between their normal duties and those of the engineer who is not there.
It is my understanding that the law requires that there must be a deckhand, who very often is a young boy, on watch on deck as well as the master or mate in the wheel-house. I suggest that regulation has been adopted for a purpose, and because of the requirement under this clause that the deckhand, master or mate must check these engine room instruments, that purpose will be lost, to say nothing of the fact that these individuals are not trained in the reading and understanding of the instruments.
When considering the whole situation which will develop as a result of the adoption of clause 9, particularly in view of the conditions which exist off the coast of British Columbia, one can only conclude that the provisions of this clause are the result of thoughtless recommendation, not only from the point of view of diminished employment but also having regard to safety.

Canada Shipping Act
1 sincerely ask the Minister of Transport to acquiesce to my suggestion that this clause be not pursued at this session, but that it be postponed until further detailed consideration has been given to it. I suggest to the minister that the officials of his department should consult fully with representatives of the national association of marine engineers of Canada. I regret very much that representatives of that association, who are vitally concerned with this subject not only from the point of view of employment but in regard to safety as well, did not have the opportunity of appearing before the standing committee which considered this bill. I do not understand why they were not invited to attend, because I know that representatives of that national association have had correspondence with officials of the minister's department for over a year. In spite of that fact they were not advised in any way by the officials of the department as to when this bill was to be considered by that standing committee of this house.
This is most unfortunate, because to my knowledge they are definitely reasonable and sensible men. I feel certain they could have contributed a good deal, and could have explained far better than I can why they are so concerned over this part of clause 9, as regards both safety and employment. In view of all the circumstances, I cannot understand why the minister would insist on this clause going through.
As I have said, this is a most serious matter to the tow boat industry in British Columbia. This committee should not be interested in the additional profits which the tow boat owners would get by laying off from 50 to 100 engineers. Our interest should be a recognition of the increased efficiency, power and automatic controls of the new diesel engines. It should be a recognition of the fact that a 24-hour watch in the engine room is required. There is a requirement for engineers who not only know their engines but also the equipment and special controls, and who have the time to check them constantly so that the salt brine, the oil and the rocking disturbance on a tow boat off the coast of British Columbia do not throw their gauges and instruments out of kilter. There should be somebody on duty 24 hours a day who knows exactly what is taking place in the engine room.
I think the association is making a most reasonable and responsible request, and I hope it will be agreed to by the minister who is in charge of piloting this bill through the committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I just say a word on the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East. I was particularly interested in

what he said because certain representations have been made to me along the lines of the subject matter on which the hon. member spoke. I learned that there has been a great deal of correspondence between the national association of marine engineers of Canada and the minister over quite a period of time dealing with the matter brought up by the hon. member for Vancouver East.
When I was approached in connection with it I asked why it was that representations were not made to the committee, and was told they did not know the committee was sitting. I can readily understand why that would be, since they live at the other end of the country in Vancouver and when the committee sat very little notice was given. I am anxious to know what answer the minister will be giving to this representation, and I hope he will find it possible to give it careful if not sympathetic consideration now.

Mr. Chairman, earlier in the discussion of this bill-and I am thinking particularly now of paragraph (c) of subclause 2 of clause 9-I expressed some concern over the application of the rule insisting on having engineers on fishing boats which were powered with engines of more than 10 nominal horsepower. First I should explain that although I recognize the need for properly qualified engineers on the larger boats which go to sea, at the same time with respect to the inshore fishing fleet consisting of small boats operating in coastal waters, which are manned by crews composed of fishermen, frequently a combination of a father and son or brothers and others, it would be very difficult, in fact it would be impossible, for those boats to have certified engineers.
However, I am glad to be informed that nominal horsepower in its relationship to brake horsepower is so varied as to be almost without relationship, if I may use that phrase. For instance, I am told that a diesel engine rated a 165 brake horsepower at 2,000 revolutions per minute, with a bore of 4.25 inches, and six cylinders would have a nominal horsepower of 1.8. I am given to understand that the nominal horsepower formula is the diameter of the cylinder squared times the number of cylinders divided by 60. A high speed engine develops its horsepower through speed rather than size, and its nominal horsepower would be lower than that of a heavy duty engine with comparatively large cylinders and low r.p.m.'s. The latter would develop its horsepower at a slower speed, and its nominal horsepower would be greater. In either case it is very unlikely that a small inshore fishing boat would have more than 10 nominal horsepower.
I was also happy to be informed that engineers for fishing boats would be rated at

least in part according to their practical experience. The only request I have to make in that connection is that some statement be made to clarify this for the public, and I have in mind in particular the fishermen in my district. I ask that this be clarified so there will be no misunderstanding of what nominal horsepower really means and what the requirements will be for engineers for fishing boats.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have just had a very interesting although not too technical observation on this matter but I do not want to get too involved in a discussion of the different types of horsepower. All I want to say is that so far as we are concerned in the department we must have fixed horsepower ratings on which to base the requirements of the act.
Brake horsepower, of course, can be influenced by revolutions and cylinder pressure, both of which can be varied at the will of the operator of an engine, and is quite unsuitable as a criterion for this reason. If we adopted brake horsepower as the criterion of measurement we could have two engines of the same size rated at different brake horsepower, because it can be varied by different revolutions. Nominal horsepower might not be so correctly indicative of the actual horsepower, but it is based on cylinder diameter and the number of cylinders, which are non-variable factors. I am just stating this to explain why we have gone by the nominal horsepower rather than the brake horsepower.
However, Mr. Chairman, at the request of the owners the department sent to the west coast an experienced marine engineer who has been aboard the tugs themselves. These tugs are now propelled by modern diesel engines, and they are fitted with a full set of automatic devices by means of which the man on the bridge can keep himself advised of what is going on in the engine room. Furthermore, the tendency toward breakdowns has been considerably reduced. Indeed, the machinery is now constructed in such a way that when repairs are necessary they can be carried out only at a site where full repair or replacement facilities exist. The report we have received from this very experienced engineer inspector leads us to believe that there is less and less necessity for an engineer to be on the watch at all times.
This is the information upon which we have acted. However, Mr. Chairman, I must say that I was impressed by the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I would not like the engineers to feel that we were pushing something on them when they had no chance to study the matter and no opportunity to appear before the 90205-6-391

committee. Of course it can be stated that this should be a matter for collective bargaining between the owners and the engineers, and I imagine that in the near future it will be. However, I hesitate to ask the committee to pass this clause. According to the hon. member the engineers had not been properly advised of the study of this matter by the committee. As hon. members know, these committee sittings are more or less last minute decisions, and it is always very difficult to give advance notice to the various people who express a desire to appear before a committee.
On the other hand, these engineers are on the west coast, rather a long distance from Ottawa. I certainly would not like it to be said that I pressed these new regulations upon the engineers, especially since they are closely related to their employment. Mr. Chairman, during the noon adjournment I had a short conversation with the hon. member for Greenwood. He said he was extremely interested in the discussion which took place during the earlier part of the morning because of the pilots who used to shoot the rapids when he lived near Kingston. I too have some very vivid recollections of this, and I wonder if I may be allowed to put on Hansard the experience of two Canadian men, Mr. T. R. Glover and Mr. D. D. Calvin, two Kingston men, so we will learn how they shot the rapids at Lachine, in the days of the drams years ago.
Presently, the long dram undulated over the first smooth rounded waves of the rapids, a moment more and we had fairly entered. As the dram hit the first big waves of the sharper descent the steersmen hauled in their oars and ran back to escape the water as it boiled over the bow of the dram, whose whole fabric bent and strained to conform to the long waves of the rapids- we dashed down the main "pitch" in what seemed no more than a few seconds. There was a curious illusion that the great barely submerged rocks were rushing upstream as we passed them; the heavy timber bumped and thudded underfoot, the water spurted up in great jets as the sides of two pieces of it struck flat together.
For those who have shot the rapids that is a most interesting and, I believe, accurate description. I raise the matter on this clause so the minister will realize what work of importance the pilots have to do in any section of the river but more particularly in this one, for the reasons I gave this morning. It strikes me that they must be highly qualified people in order to carry through these difficult waters ships of the kind, length and draft mentioned earlier.
I wonder whether the minister would not give consideration to treating this clause in the same way as he dealt with clause No. 9. I am sure that the pilots and those who sit on this side of the house would be very grateful to him if this clause were withdrawn for the time being, until a definite arrangement on it is made with the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I think there is a wide difference between the two clauses. With respect to clause 9 a major aspect of employment arose. My impression is that the employment of a number of engineers on the west coast was at stake, and also that these engineers or their association did not have an opportunity to express their views before the committee. With regard to clause 15, as far as the pilots in the Cornwall district are concerned no question of employment or of salary arises. Also, I think the pilots themselves or their representatives appeared before the committee and had all the opportunity in the world to express their views, to be questioned and to give their opinions on the
[The Deputy Chairman.!
whole matter. I therefore think there is a great difference between the two clauses. I really believe that clause 15 will not hurt the pilots. It is not unfair to anybody. I believe it will not hurt anyone either now or in the future.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The pilots, of course, do not agree with that statement. As the minister knows, they made representations against it and they made their position quite clear. However, I am not going to pursue the matter other than to ask one or two questions, if I may do so. Can the minister tell me why this section was not included in chapter 40 of last year's statutes which introduced a new section, namely the pilotage section, as an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act? Why was it not introduced at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: The amendment last year dealt purely with great lakes waters. The Cornwall-Montreal district is one that deals only with strictly Canadian waters. That is the reason it was not included.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is Canada getting anything in exchange for this concession to United States vessels?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Quite lengthy discussions have taken place between our officials and United States officials. As is well known, as to pilotage in the great lakes, the St. Lawrence river and practically everywhere else in the world, very complicated and very technical matters are always involved. My officials and the United States officials carried on lengthy discussions and both sides tried to act in a most fair way.
We obtained some extremely advantageous results as far as we were concerned. One that comes to my mind is with regard to the lake Michigan area, which was not restricted. These are purely United States waters. I could say that this is an example of give and take or of the consideration that the United States has given to us. Also they have been very co-operative in determining the number of United States pilots who are going to be brought into the picture. They could have asked that on the great lakes half of the piloting be done by United States pilots and half by Canadian pilots. Instead of doing that they accepted a gradual increase in the proportion over a period of five years. They did that instead of asking for it immediately. I think those are fairly important considerations on top of all the others I mentioned this morning.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
One of the considerations the minister has just mentioned is that compulsory pilotage will be exempted for Canadian vessels on lake Michigan, which is purely a United States lake. My question is

this. Has the United States congress enacted legislation similar to that which the Canadian parliament is now considering?

In the agreement on pilotage between the two countries the lake Michigan area was expressly exempted, or rather the exemption was withdrawn in favour of Canadians and it was expressed in that agreement. I am also informed that it is provided for in the United States legislation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have the great lakes pilotage agreement, and in it there seems to be no reference to lake Michigan.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: 1 am informed that lake Michigan is designated in the agreement. I have not the agreement at hand, but I am informed by my officials that lake Michigan is mentioned in it, that the waters of lake Michigan are considered as designated waters and that Canadian pilots may operate in the designated waters.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Can the minister point to the legislation passed by congress which exempts Canadian ships from pilotage dues on lake Michigan?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

speechtext:
At the time this matter was last under discussion, the Minister of Justice gave an explanation as to why the government could not accept or take any action on my recommendation concerning voluntary commitment. I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare intends to say something about this matter, and for that reason I should like to take a couple of minutes of the committee's time before he speaks.
I was quite intrigued by the main argument that was used by the Minister of Justice in opposing the proposal relating to voluntary commitment for the treatment of narcotic addicts. He used, as an example, the mental health laws. He cited the fact that if one were mentally ill one had to be committed for treatment by law. I thought that in putting forth that argument he killed his own line of reasoning. I do not know what the legislative provisions are across Canada relating to mental health, but I do know the provisions in British Columbia. Up until a few years ago if one were mentally ill, the only way the individual could be handled was to have him committed to the mental institution by law. He was either committed by the order of a magistrate and one doctor who was obliged to sign the committal papers or he was committed by the signature of two doctors. However, that is not the situation now. If a person is suffering from a mental disability he is not obliged, automatically and axiomatically, to go through the process of being committed to the institution as an insane person. He can have a voluntary commitment, a commitment whereby the person knows that he requires treatment just the same as the person who has a certain condition in the way of disease or broken bones knows he must have treatment.
In British Columbia-and I am just using this province as an example because I know so well the situation and the legislation- instead of having to go under the impact of the law and be committed as an insane person, on examination by a doctor who feels that person requires some treatment for a mental disorder the person can, on the examination and recognition of the doctor, voluntarily sign himself or herself into the Crease clinic, just the same as at a general hospital for an acute disease or disability. He signs himself into a specific clinic of psychological medicine. It is all in the same area as the mental hospital but it is an entirely different building. On a doctor's recommendation, as I say, he voluntarily commits himself.

If, when I was speaking of voluntary commitment the Minister of Justice or the Minister of National Health and Welfare was under the impression that I thought he could just walk in and say, "I am a narcotic addict and I want treatment", let me say at once that I did not mean that at all. What I meant was this. If a person is a narcotic addict and wants to get that monkey off his back, to use an expression which I used the other day and which is common in the terminology of an addict; and if he sees a doctor and the doctor examines him and says that he is an addict, then the question I ask is this. Instead of the situation being as it will be without change in this present bill No. C-100, namely that of having to be actually under the Criminal Code or under this act picked up, committed and sentenced, why can there not be something whereby we can have a voluntary commitment as a narcotic addict, as we now have it in British Columbia and I believe in many of the other provinces, a commitment on a voluntary basis without going through that stigma, shall I say, of a commitment basically and actually under the law?
I just want to emphasize, as I tried to do the other day, that to many people a great deal depends upon a psychological attitude and approach. I feel most strongly that, where we have those who want to help themselves to be cured, there should be in our law some means whereby they can do it, or some provision that will differentiate between them and those whom the law is obliged to pick up and to compel to go through treatment. I feel quite strongly about this matter. I feel quite certain that I am correct about the psychological viewpoint of that type of person. When the minister speaks on this matter I hope he will tell us whether or not, on review, it is possible to cover that aspect which I feel to be of such great importance.

I regret that I was not able to be here when this bill was introduced. I should like to say a few words on this bill which I, along with other members in this committee, strongly support. It surprised me a little bit that the initiative in this

matter seemed to have been taken by the Minister of Justice. By saying that I am not implying that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has not shown great interest in this matter. However, it always puzzled me why, in a matter of this sort involving essentially matters having to do with the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Minister of Justice should have emerged as the spokesman for the administration. The first public intimation that was given of this measure was when the Minister of Justice was in British Columbia about two years ago. There, at a press conference, he announced the government's intention to proceed with legislation of this kind. At the time I suggested to the minister that I hoped this was a matter about which he had carefully consulted the Minister of National Health and Welfare because it was a matter that concerned the Department of National Health and Welfare in a large degree, although not entirely. I am therefore glad that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is here today to assume the functions that were so clandestinely and later so demonstrably taken away from him by the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext: Don't overdo it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
I think this bill marks a progressive step forward. The Minister of National Health and Welfare will have had the opportunity of having a great deal of background material in the department on this matter. He will have had the valuable experience of his officials, particularly the deputy minister and the solicitor of the department. In the bill there are some features that cause me to ask some questions and also to make one or two observations.
The idea of detention, as is provided in clause 15 of the bill, is I think an important and desirable step. However, if we are going to make fully effective the policy that is revealed in this bill I think we shall have to appreciate the fact that certain things not covered in the bill will have to be done. I am sure both ministers have had an opportunity, either directly or vicariously, of learning of the work that is being done in this field in Lexington, Kentucky by the government of the United States. I myself had the opportunity of visiting that institution with officials of the department, of ascertaining the extent of the success of the experiment there and also of learning of some of the inadequacies not of the care provided but of some of the follow-up practices which are not as effective as they might be.
It cannot be said that the detention, imposed or voluntary, of a drug addict in an institution such as that in Lexington is necessarily 100 per cent effective. One of the 90205-6-392
Narcotic Drug Control
reasons is the inadequate follow-up system that is or at least was practised in that institution. Under this bill it is not contemplated that one found guilty of trafficking in drugs shall necessarily spend his full life in an institution. If that was contemplated by the use of the word "indeterminate" there would be cause for further interrogation.
It would be interesting to learn from the Minister of National Health and Welfare what system will be used to follow up cases of drug addicts detained under the provisions of this act following judicial determination. The problem in this country is not as great as it is in the United States, because we have relatively fewer addicts. I think we have some 3,000 drug addicts in Canada.
If we are going to do an effective job in providing for treatment and rehabilitation while these people are detained, knowing the number of cases where drug addicts resort to their former practice after having abandoned it while being detained, we will want to establish an effective follow-up system.
The provincial governments have a responsibility in this matter and indeed they can play a very great part. After all, the health services of the federal government are limited in so far as treatment facilities are concerned. Under the provinces are to be found the most effective and efficient methods of providing for the health care of the people of our country. A policy of decentralization in that regard is the pattern of our country. I am sure no one wishes to disturb that.
It would be interesting to know what the prospects are for provincial co-operation, particularly from the provinces where the largest numbers of drug addicts are to be found. For instance, is the province of British Columbia prepared to co-operate in some way? If it did co-operate it could meet the point which the hon. member for Vancouver East has just raised.
With regard to voluntary commitment, I must say that in principle I fully share the hon. member's concern and his objective, as I think do most hon. members. The proposal is that individuals who have been found guilty of drug trafficking and who are placed in detention will serve the punishment provided for under the act but at the same time, it is presumed, because of the general statement made by the minister, they will be given curative attention; they will receive the rehabilitation processes that have been devised for users of drugs.
This will be a form of care which will cost some money, but wholly justifiable. We do not want unnecessary duplication if we can avoid doing so. It seems to me that, depending upon the type of institution, it would

Narcotic Drug Control
be wise for the provinces to co-operate fully, rather than to set up a series of institutions to serve a limited population.
If an individual suffering from drug addiction who had not committed a crime wishes to take advantage of this treatment, it seems to me there ought to be means provided to bring that about. I think one of the difficulties is the constitutional difficulty. In so far as this parliament is concerned there may be difficulty, under this act, in making it legislatively possible for an individual to receive treatment in such an institution. I doubt that the parliament of Canada would have the power-and perhaps the Minister of Justice will give us his views about this-to provide that an individual who had not committed a crime and who was not being charged with a crime in connection with trafficking should be placed in an institution, pursuant to a federal act.

Yes, that is the reason, but often times when there is the repeal of an act an explanation is given of the differences between the two acts. In any event, there are no explanatory notes at all in this bill. When we come to the various clauses we will indicate how valuable this might have been.
I am sure there is wide approval of the general purposes of this bill. The bill will go a long way in the treatment of drug addicts, I am sure, even though the experiment of their treatment in institutions is not as yet a fully established fact. If we have the kind of follow-up system that is necessary, this could be an important reform and an important step forward.
The government has our full support in the initiative it has taken, but I would simply point out that if this follow-up is not pursued, much of the good will be lost, as I am sure the minister's officials would confirm. I have seen records of individuals in the institution at Lexington who had left the institution after a period of two years fully cured and fully relieved of the terrible disability under which they suffered. I have known other cases where as a result of a failure to follow this thing through, people have left the institution, gone out into the community and then reverted to their former habits of addiction.
The hon. member himself drew an analogy in terms of people receiving treatment for mental illness. As we all know, in the case of mental illness today the process of cure and rehabilitation does not end when a patient is discharged from an institution. Many people, after a period of confinement, are allowed to live outside where social workers and others follow their cases through and

give the help and guidance which are necessary. There are other cases where the patient never enters a mental institution; all the necessary treatment is carried on outside. Supervision of this kind is necessary, in my opinion, in order to make this act effective and if the minister can give us some information in this regard I am sure the committee will be interested.
It may be that the minister has in mind that the necessary supervision must be left to the provincial authorities. I can understand that, and it may be the best arrangement because of the difficulty of trying to supervise from the centre. Perhaps the ministers have the idea that the supervision will take place from the central institution provided under this act. In any event, these are points which engage our interest and which justify our understandable curiosity with regard to a measure which, I believe, deserves our full support.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
Before clause 1 carries I should like to make a further statement. In reply to the hon. member for Essex East, I hope he does not think that the remarks he made at the beginning of his observations will prevent the Minister of Justice and myself from playing golf together or any such thing. We do not want to get angry at each other. Maybe the hon. gentleman has been carried away by his feelings to an undue extent, because he must have boycotted the speech made by the Minister of Justice on second reading in which my colleague set out in some detail the answers to some of the questions the hon. member has been asking.
In the bill, under the definition clause, "minister" means, with respect to part I, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and with respect to part II, the Minister of Justice. Clause 15, as the hon. member will see, is the first clause in part II and it is only logical, I think, that treatment, after this stage has been reached, should come under the Minister of Justice because he has responsibility for handling the institutions; the parole board comes under the Department of Justice, and so on. I know that if there are any further questions about this part of the bill the Minister of Justice will be glad to answer them.
I should like now to say a few words about the discussion we were having on Wednesday last when the house rose. At that time we were discussing the question of facilities for the reception on a voluntary basis of narcotic addicts who desired treatment and who did not come within the provisions of this bill. My colleague the Minister of Justice clearly explained the purpose of the control 90205-6-3924
Narcotic Drug Control
measures provided by this measure in connection with treatment. He also pointed out that the treatment of non-criminal addicts would be a matter entirely within the scope of provincial legislative authority.
It is understood, of course, that if a province enacts complementary legislation, a narcotic addict could voluntarily subject himself to committal procedure and thus secure the benefit of treatment. I gather, however, that what hon. members may have had in mind is some form of treatment program on a wholly voluntary basis that would not involve a formal committal procedure.
When he spoke a few minutes ago I believe the hon. member for Vancouver East corrected the impression which had been drawn from his earlier remarks in this respect. But I should like to go on and assure the committee of my support for and co-operation in any treatment program that may be provided under responsible and experienced auspices. This would, of course, include, to the extent necessary, medical supervision. We would be very glad to give consideration to any proposals which might be advanced in this regard, and would certainly contribute the benefit of our knowledge and experience to the furtherance of their success.
However, I would point out that there are certain difficulties which appear to be inherent in what may be described as a voluntary treatment program. I refer here to the necessity for the right of legal control of the individual undergoing treatment. It is the view of my department that desirable as it may be that an individual should be encouraged to seek treatment, if treatment is to be effective there must be a legal right to continue it for such period as is necessary. In other words, while voluntary application for treatment is an important factor as indicating a necessary motivation by the individual, there must be some means of ensuring that treatment does not wholly depend on the continuation of such motivation. Some provision must be made to the end that treatment can be carried on even though the addict himself feels he has reached the point where he no longer needs it.
While there has not hitherto been available in Canada any intensive or comprehensive treatment program for narcotic addicts, treatment has been available on a limited basis through a number of facilities. In many instances, these facilities have been privately operated. I am advised, however, that it has been the experience of those concerned with such institutions that although a person should be encouraged to accept voluntary commitment, there must be some form of

Narcotic Drug Control
legal procedure which would prevent him from discontinuing treatment whenever he wished.
I think the reasons for this are self-evident and I am sure hon. members would agree there is nothing unfair or prejudicial to an individual in requiring him to submit to treatment for whatever period of time competent authorities may feel is required.
While the expression "voluntary treatment" suggests a proper and humane approach to the problem, experience strongly suggests that the motivation of the individual addict sometimes needs critical examination. In some instances, this may stem merely from a desire to reduce a habit that has become too costly to support. Here there is clearly a necessity for legal control.
In other cases, the addict's motivation, though satisfactory in the first instance, may tend to disappear once withdrawal has been accomplished. Cessation of treatment at that point would not likely lead to continued abstinence from drugs and, therefore, no useful purpose would be served if he could discontinue at will.
These conclusions, I might add, are in accordance with views expressed by competent authorities at a conference held in the city of Vancouver in 1952 at which were represented various levels of interest in the problem of addiction in the community. They are also in line with the thinking of authorities in charge of the narcotic treatment hospital at Lexington, Kentucky, to which the hon. member for Essex East referred a moment ago, as well as of New York state authorities who are presently undertaking treatment programs on an experimental basis. As late as last Friday afternoon, as expressed during discussions that my officials had with New York state authorities, it was still their point of view that they must have legal control.
I can assure the committee that my department has been actively concerned with all aspects of treatment as it is currently being considered in various parts of the United States and in this country. In addition to maintaining direct liaison with authorities in various areas where experimentation in treatment is being carried out, our officials also work through the mental health advisory committee which is assisted by a special subcommittee on drug addiction.
A year ago, this subcommittee set up a working party under the chairmanship of Dr. Halliday who was referred to in this debate as the head of the British Columbia narcotic addiction foundation. This working party is charged with the task of examining and reporting on treatment and other health

aspects of addiction and, to my mind, points up the active and continuing interest being shown in this problem.
We would not be optimistic of the success of a program that was based solely on the voluntary desire of an addict and that was not accompanied by some right of custodial control. Moreover, we feel that the measures contemplated by this bill in leading to committal under provincial legislation for the purpose of treatment, do not depart substantially from those which would be necessary in any proper treatment program. It is our view that regardless of whether treatment is carried out in the institutions which are now being proposed or in institutions unrelated to those covered by this bill, the factor of compulsory detention and supervision would seem to be equally a requisite.
It goes without saying that any province would be free to institute a special treatment program separate and apart from that which this measure proposes. It could also count on our wholehearted co-operation in contributing whatever knowledge and experience that might be pertinent in making such a program successful.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister would permit me to ask a question at this point. If the provinces set up institutions of that kind, is the minister prepared to say now whether he could offer financial assistance under the national health program?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I was just about to refer to that subject.
In certain circumstances, it might even be possible for the dominion government to provide some financial assistance under the health grants program. Any project in this regard would, of course, have to be submitted through the province to receive consideration. I must say that if we were asked to provide assistance to a purely voluntary program, we would feel obliged to draw attention to the aspects of control and supervision to which I have made reference. This would not, however, preclude our helping to the greatest extent possible in any experimental project on a voluntary basis. Certainly, there is need for more research and experimentation than up to now has been carried out.
In this connection, I would like to conclude by quoting from a recent paper published in the New York state "Journal of Medicine". It is written by Dr. Larimore, deputy commissioner of the New York state department of health and Dr. Brill of the New York state department of mental hygiene, and covers their investigation of the so-called British treatment system with particular reference to

the need for further research. Speaking of the situation in the United Kingdom, the authors had this to say:
There is general scepticism about the effectiveness of existing methods of treatment, as well as a general dissatisfaction with the long term results which are generally described as marked by a very large proportion of recidivism or relapse-
Placing the patient in a hospital for withdrawal is certainly sound. Beyond that, in the treatment of the underlying condition, it must be recognized that neither we nor the British have at the present time a satisfactory treatment method for narcotic addiction.
Nevertheless there are a number of important reasons to believe that addiction is treatable and that better methods should be sought since "spontaneous cures" do occur, especially with increasing maturity, and it is a well known fact that older narcotic addicts are far fewer in number than young ones.
Further, some cases respond even to present treatment methods. However, the development of more successful treatment must await the results of research-
In both the United Kingdom and the United States, there is strong agreement as to the need for much basic research to be done in this field. Because of recent advancements in chemical and other technologies and in the theory of psychiatric drugs, there is better reason than ever before to expect constructive results from research.
I would just like to emphasize, in respect to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East about treatment centres, that we certainly feel the provinces can do this at any time they wish without conditions being attached. It is our view that this is a separate discipline. Over the years we have received requests, as has the Minister of Justice, from individuals and organizations for help in regard to treatment along the lines we have advanced.
Mr. Chairman, I should like personally to congratulate the Minister of Justice for proposing this new concept of assisting and curing, if possible, narcotic addicts. I should also like to pay tribute to the late Mr. E. P. Winch, the father of the hon. member for Vancouver East. It was evident from a review of old files only last week that this gentleman while a member of the legislative assembly for British Columbia, was perhaps the first to suggest the establishment of treatment centres and that he urged consideration in this regard many, many times.
I feel that is all I need to say at the moment Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before making any comment in regard to the statement which the minister has just made, may I express my great appreciation of his kind remarks in relation to the studies and work that were undertaken by my late father some 25 years ago, when he was a member of the British Columbia legislature.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Narcotic Drug Control

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
It is because of the work which he did in that field, as well as in others, that I know I can safely say that irrespective of politics, he is revered by all who knew him in British Columbia.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to what the minister has had to say this afternoon. The viewpoint which he has put forward places emphasis on the remarks made the other day by the Minister of Justice, but I must say he has not convinced me as yet. I am quite certain there are not insurmountable obstacles in the way of achieving what I have suggested.
In regard to his remarks about separate provincial institutions being established for the treatment of addicts on a voluntary basis, I should like to think them over before I come to any decision. I feel quite honestly that, in view of the expenditures which the taxpayer must make through the federal treasury in order to handle this problem in providing the expert professional care which is required, and the building of the institutions, I am not certain whether there is any clear foundation for duplication in this field.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member will allow me to continue for a moment or two, following which I shall answer his questions if I am able to.
I believe we must pay special attention to this question so as to avoid duplication. I am not yet convinced that a plan could not be worked out, but I do wish to emphasize immediately I completely agree that even if a method of voluntary commitment is worked out on some basis, whether federally, provincially or jointly, before a person goes into any institution for treatment of a corrective nature for narcotic addiction it can only be done on a legal basis under which the person is accepted under certain controls, regulations, discipline, timing and care. I do not know of anything in the constitution or in law under which that can be done as part and parcel of the availability of the opportunity to take curative treatment in an institution by a person who volunteers to go in. Therefore I say, sir, I do not think this is an insurmountable obstacle in any way, although it has been raised by the minister.
One could speak for a long time on this and be repetitive; therefore I am not going to comment any more on it. I do not think I can add anything to what I said the other day or to what I said today.
With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise just one other matter before I sit down because I think I can only raise it in the discussion of clause 1. I regret

Narcotic Drug Control
that I cannot be here this evening. I know this is my responsibility but I do feel that since I have been at the United Nations I owe the courtesy of my attendance at the dinner tonight in honour of the president of the United Nations. Therefore I hope you will not mind, sir, if I change the subject at this time.
I think a great many of us in the committee, and particularly members from British Columbia, would appreciate it very much if the Minister of Justice could give us a clearer picture of the basis of his thinking on the establishment of narcotic treatment centres. We would appreciate it if he could give us as fully as possible his view of the basis upon which they are to be established. I do not have to reiterate to him my interest in this matter and my desires. If I am wrong I should like to be told so, but I should like to know why in the announcement made by the minister through the provincial member for Chilliwack there is to be a $5 million institution built at Matsqui. It is not the location at Matsqui that I am interested in, it is the institution itself and that is what I should like the minister to comment on. Statements are being made by those interested in this matter in British Columbia. Editorials of a somewhat critical nature are being written. I am not going to comment on whether they are right or wrong. That is what I want the minister to discuss. The Minister of Justice, together with the Minister of National Health and Welfare, are now breaking new ground on this question of narcotic addiction and how it should be approached. Undoubtedly mistakes will be made. We shall never get anywhere if we are afraid of making mistakes. I am certain that the two ministers and all of us are prepared to learn by mistakes and we are prepared to make some. We realize that this is a new field of endeavour and that a great many troubles will have to be faced. But why, in the breaking of this new ground, has it been decided to erect a $5 million institution-if this figure is correct and I presume it is because it was given out by the member for that area-on the information and authority of the Minister of Justice? Is there a good reason why this policy is being followed? Is there a better reason to move perhaps-and this may sound amazing coming from me-a little bit slower, to feel our way, to see how it works? Then if you need a larger institution you have the experience upon which to move.
I believe that some of the questions being asked in the editorials are good. I hope that the Minister of Justice has not, all of a sudden perhaps, been overcome a little by the magnitude of the great task which he and the Minister of National Health and Welfare

are undertaking. I hope that some of his officials-and I have one particularly in mind who I know likes to do things on a grand scale-have not influenced the minister too much in this direction. I can see that the minister knows the individual in his department to whom I am referring. I do hope that he will give us a policy statement and as detailed a picture as possible on how they decided on the magnitude of this particular institution which has already been announced, and why the thing was handled in that way instead of perhaps, as I said before, feeling the way before such a terrific expenditure is made on one institution.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question now with regard to the point he made on duplication of facilities and the fact that he thought this would be perhaps wasteful of the taxpayer's dollar if it was not carried out all the way by the federal government. Would he not agree that we in British Columbia already have facilities which can take care of voluntary committals and which as we know do have psychiatric and skilled medical staff to handle the particular problem of drug addicts? We already have means of voluntary committals at the Crease clinic at Essondale.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
No, I am afraid not. I believe the hon. member when he spoke made reference to the narcotic foundation. The narcotic foundation in British Columbia is doing a wonderful job and should have received much more support than it has received up to now.
The hon. member referred to the Crease clinic. I say that this is not the answer because although there can be voluntary committal to the Crease clinic for certain disorders after consultation with a doctor, a person can only stay a certain length of time in the Crease clinic. Unless they have changed the regulations since I was a member of the legislature the period is three months. That is what it was when the act was passed. As the hon. member knows, I was leader of the opposition at that time. It is only a temporary stay for curative purposes if you can be handled. It is only of a temporary nature. I can assure the hon. member from my knowledge of narcotic addicts that you do not in the majority of cases bring about a cure, especially anything of a lasting nature, in a matter of three months. A longer period of time than that is required. As a general rule I believe it is well over one year. I believe, if I heard correctly a little while ago, the hon. member for Essex East said the treatment had to be conducted for a period of from one year to three years and then the doctors are not always completely

sure. So I say that the Crease clinic very definitely is not the answer. I doubt very much if they receive very many in that institution with a narcotic drug problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
Perhaps I should answer the questions asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East and referred to by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, because I would not want some of the things that have been said about this new centre to go unanswered. I do recall that at the very end of the debate on Wednesday of last week I had reached some of the comments that had already been made out on the west coast. I said that to me it seemed to be a pretty peremptory dismissal of a far-reaching new proposal to say, as the party of my friend in British Columbia did, that it was altogether quite wrong and a proven failure. In so far as I have not even seen the plans for this building as yet because they have not been completed, I am quite sure that Mr. Barrett, a C.C.F. member of the legislature in British Columbia, has not seen the plans or had any discussions about the proposal.
I notice there is a doctor in Vancouver who is reported to be an expert in the field, and who has also condemned the institution in a telephone call from Montreal to a British Columbia newspaper. Dr. Tyhurst has not telephoned me as yet, so I do not know the real basis of his objection. I do want to make it clear that in devising this plan, in devising the details of the custody for treatment program, the officials of my department have had lengthy discussions with officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare. This department is constantly in touch with capable and thoughtful people in this field, as well as having capable and thoughtful officials in their own service. In addition, the

Narcotic Drug Control
officials of my department, particularly the commissioner of penitentiaries and other members of the correctional planning committee, who first began the study of the development of the federal institutional program to treat narcotic addicts rather than merely incarcerate them, themselves had discussions in the course of their study with senior correctional officers in California, where we are informed they are now developing a plan much along the same lines as we have here envisaged. They also had discussions with officials, psychiatrists and psychologists and other persons in Vancouver interested in the problem, including members of the university staff. I understand that Dr. Tyhurst is head of the University of British Columbia department of psychiatry. Apparently Dr. Tyhurst was not one of those with whom the committee consulted in Vancouver two years ago, but other representatives of the university were consulted.
I am not in a position at the moment to give a blueprint of this institution because we have not drawn up the plans as yet. We are consulting architects now and of course we will lay down, in consultation with the Department of National Health and Welfare, the general design and purpose of the institution and ask the architects to produce the plan of a building which will carry those purposes into effect.
In so far as the location at Matsqui is concerned, may I say that I have learned it is only some 50 minutes from the centre of downtown Vancouver. This could hardly be said to be remote. The route of the new trans-Canada highway, according to our information, is going to pass Matsqui. I am told that a journey of 45 minutes, at the maximum, from downtown Vancouver will take one to the institution. There are many people in our cities today who spend far more than 45 minutes struggling to and from work. I do not believe we are really putting obstacles in the way of any professional person who desires to come there to assist us or in the way of the members of the narcotic foundation if they want to get in touch with the treatment centre at Matsqui. We feel, however, that we must have the institution physically removed from downtown Vancouver, if for no other reason than that we do want to have some element of control over the persons who pass by and who may thus introduce narcotics into the institution.
You cannot have an institution of this kind located in downtown Vancouver with the kind of drug trafficking and organized trafficking that we know exists, and expect to successfully keep narcotics from being smuggled into the institution. I would not guarantee that we can completely prevent it at Matsqui,

but we will have a better chance of controlling things around the periphery so people will not have a chance of caching narcotics, then picking up the caches and getting them inside, than if it were in a huge city.
As to the criticism that it is going to be too big-that is, that it is too big and will have too many inmates-may I say that it has never been our intention simply to have an institution in which some 400 narcotic addicts are all treated on an identical pattern. The institution might well be capable-and this we have in mind-of operating on the basis of separate clinical units with perhaps 80 patients or 100 patients or inmates in each unit. Just because it is going to be physically capable of housing perhaps 400 or more people, it does not mean that we have decided that every one of those inmates is going to receive absolutely equal treatment. In planning the institution we have in mind that it should be so designed that it can be capable of being operated in smaller units, although all contained in the same general area.
I think I should just say that one purpose at least which it will achieve is the segregation of all the criminal drug addicts in British Columbia from the non-criminal addicts. Not until we have done that can we really start treatment programs on, to some extent, an experimental basis and it will have to be on an experimental basis because no compulsory treatment program has ever before been designed or attempted in Canada. The first requisite therefore is segregation. Then we can test out the treatment program and develop it as we along. That is absolutely impossible to do under the present circumstances.
We intend to proceed on an experimental basis. We intend to consult extensively and continuously with the experts in this field; I refer to the medical and psychiatric experts. We are not going to go blindly ahead on the assumption that we can draw up a blueprint of treatment without consultation; of course we are not going to do that. May I point out that this building will not possibly be ready for complete operation within a matter of two years. It has only just been decided where the location is to be. There is plenty of time for consultation and for us to learn and to acquire the additional benefit of the views of others over and above those with whom, as I have pointed out and emphasized, our officials have already discussed the matter.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext: No. It is not envisaged that they would be kept in the institution at Matsqui for the whole time until they are pronounced fit subjects to be released from institutional custody and then turned out and sent back to Vancouver with no acclimatization as it were.
