speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make one or two remarks on this particular clause, primarily on the question of the punishment of life imprisonment. During discussion on the recent amendments to the Criminal Code I think it was fairly clearly pointed out to the house that we were retaining the death penalty in some instances because it was a deterrent to the crime of murder.
In 1960 I introduced a bill amending the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. At that time I tried to distinguish between a user and a non-user of narcotics for the purpose of trafficking and suggested there should be a sentence of death or imprisonment for life imposed for this offence.
The thing that concerns me particularly about the clause now before us is that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, in his earlier remarks when referring to the Senate committee, said as reported at page 5980 of Hansard for June 7:
The report of the Senate committee recommended that trafficking, regardless of its purpose, should be made a costly and hazardous undertaking in terms of a penalty. While the Senate committee did recommend that there be mandatory minimums for second or subsequent offences for trafficking, it was the view of the enforcement authorities that a more effective deterrent would lie in the increase of the maximum penalty and that the courts should be empowered to impose within the framework of a lengthy maximum what might be an appropriate penalty for trafficking.
The minister went on to say:
The sentence which may be imposed has been raised to life imprisonment. In this way parliament will have indicated clearly the seriousness with which it regards trafficking offences and the courts can, therefore, take cognizance of this in fixing appropriate penalties.
The Miniser of Justice is reported at page 5986 of Hansard as having made the following statement:
The law relating to the suppression of trafficking, then, should be sufficient in terms of punishment reasonably to deter the would-be trafficker from engaging in that form of activity and, if it does not do so, it should be adequate to protect society against him when he persists.
I was very impressed by the statements made by the hon. member for Vancouver East, who has been noted in this house as an abolitionist. At page 5994 of Hansard he is reported as having said:


There is also the clause that deals with trafficking. I am discussing it only in principle. A person can have no sympathy for one who breaks the law, no sympathy at all for one who commits homicide and, of course, no sympathy for one who traffics in narcotics. I think about the lowest depths that any man or woman can sink to is to be a trafficker in narcotics. A murderer kills and that is it. But one who traffics in drugs, who brings a person to addiction, to that insatiable craziness, makes an absolute hourly and daily hell for life for the addict. I, therefore, have no sympathy for him, and I agree that for the trafficker there should be a penalty of up to life.
I would point out that the hon. member said quite clearly, following up his philosophy, that there should be a penalty of up to life, but I felt-and I am putting my own interpretation on his words-that he came very close to advocating the death sentence for this offence.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext: No. That will be the day.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
The point that concerns me is this. A survey was recently made by the narcotic addiction foundation. They sent out questionnaires to over 339 young people in Vancouver. I understand the questionnaire was not limited to particular areas where narcotics are a problem. The findings of this survey are quite interesting. For example, 19.5 per cent of the 18 year olds said they had an opportunity to use heroin, and some 50 per cent of those in the 15-18 years of age category said they had an opportunity to use heroin while they were drinking.
In the last two years the narcotic addiction foundation has treated some 285 patients. Of that number 45 per cent of the males and 48 per cent of the females were drug addicts by the age of 20 years. I am concerned that these very, very young people are exposed to the dangers of drugs. I feel that a trafficker who is either a user or a non-user himself- and I think it is more serious in the case of the non-user-should be subject to the maximum deterrent.
Logically, since we said in connection with the amendments to the Criminal Code that capital punishment was a deterrent to somebody who wanted to commit a robbery, for example, or to various types of minder, it seems to me that we have here the most obvious case for the maximum deterrent. I say this because in the case of a trafficker, especially in the case of a trafficker who is a non-user, the prime incentive is the monetary return that he gets. I think in these circumstances we are justified in imposing the maximum deterrent, which is the sentence of death.
Accordingly I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway:
That clause 4 (3) be amended by adding after the word "life" in line six, the words "or sentenced to death".

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I could not help but note with interest the tact that the mover of this amendment quoted some of the remarks I made the other day. I want the hon. member and this committee to know that I meant every word I said. There is no question whatsoever in my mind that one of the most heinous crimes which can be committed is the illicit trafficking of narcotic drugs.
I agree with the hon. member that the worst of these traffickers is the non-user, because he is motivated wholly and solely by the profit motive. That was the reason why during my remarks last week I added to the words used by the Minister of Justice "demand and supply", the words "and profit". I pointed out that I thought if we could by this bill directly, or in co-operation with the provinces, wipe out the profit motive we would take a major step forward in wiping out the entire narcotics problem.
However, I think the hon. member and the committee know that I still stand in complete opposition to the death penalty. I think it is inhuman, unchristian, unnecessary and is no deterrent. I know, from speaking to many people who have been serving terms of life imprisonment that a life sentence is a pretty horrible thing to contemplate. These people are under regimentation every hour of their lives and are denied meeting with society.
In speaking to the amendment directly, if my memory is correct there is only one country in the world which has the death penalty for drug trafficking, and that is Iran. In the not too distant past Iran was one of the greatest producers of narcotic drugs for illicit trafficking. Iran also had one of the largest percentages of population in the world of people who were addicts. I am speaking from memory, but I believe that only about three years ago they had in the neighbourhood of 325,000 known addicts in Iran. That is why in 1959 Iran took a major step forward and opened up treatment clinics for drug addicts. In two years 65,000 addicts have been treated in these clinics. But they also provided the death penalty as the ultimate punishment for any key person who was engaged in the growing or illicit trafficking of narcotics.
I had the opportunity of speaking to two of the cabinet ministers from Iran this year at the United Nations. They have been able to make great steps forward, but they have found they can get results without having to resort to the death penalty. I am sorry that after the progressive thoughts which have been expressed by the hon. member he should be so reactionary and retrogressive as to move this amendment.
Narcotic Drug Control

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
We
have had a good deal of discussion in the house on capital punishment in the last year or so. I do not think the argument put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver East should carry too much weight in this debate, because the house did not accept his views on capital punishment before, and he has added nothing to them at this time.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext: It has gone a long way, though.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
I am
one of those who held strong views in favour of the retention of the death penalty. However, after listening to a number of other members express the view that for certain kinds of murder capital punishment is no deterrent I felt I could support the government measure brought forward exempting certain crimes from the death penalty.
Nevertheless, the hon. member for Vancouver East has agreed that the trafficker in narcotics is at least as bad as the worst type of murderer, and the other members of this house believe that the worst type of murderer should be sentenced to death. Thus I think he has put forward a fair argument for saying that a trafficker in narcotics should be sentenced to death. The hon. member does not believe a trafficker should be sentenced to death, because he does not believe murderers should be sentenced to death; but the rest of the house believes they should be sentenced to death.
I think the hon. member was wrong in saying there was only one country which prescribed the death penalty-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext: I said there was only one to my knowledge.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
I
noticed an article in the Globe and Mail of November 19, 1960 entitled "Dope Pushers Face Death". It read:
Bangkok. Nov. 16 (Reuters)-Heroin and morphine manufacturers and peddlers face the death sentence or life imprisonment under a bill approved by the Thai cabinet today.
This seems to be a growing problem. A murderer does, of course, cause the death of a person but a trafficker in narcotics may ruin the lives of several people, perhaps of hundreds. Having accepted the view that capital punishment is a unique deterrent and that it should be retained in Canada I suggest there is no more suitable course for the house to take than to apply it to those who traffic in narcotics and I wholeheartedly support the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond. I hope it will be accepted by the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
I feel I should say now that the government, while appreciating fully the

Narcotic Drug Control sentiments of the hon. members who have spoken in support of this amendment, is unable to accept it. This is not because we disagree with them as to the despicable nature of the crime of trafficking in narcotics, particularly when engaged in for motives of profit and not, for instance, to support a craving arising from personal addiction. The trafficker who is not himself an addict and who puts this substance into circulation deserves condemnation in language stronger than one could devise to describe him.
The fact of the matter is that we have decided, and recommended to the house, and the house has approved, that generally speaking the grounds for capital punishment should be restricted rather than enlarged. I know that it is still a potential penalty for those guilty of treason or piracy but broadly speaking capital punishment is now restricted to those who kill as a result of planning and deliberation. We think it would be completely inconsistent with that principle to enlarge the types of crimes to which capital punishment is now applicable so as to include trafficking in narcotics.
May I remind the committee that not very long ago the penalty for trafficking, for whatever purpose, was seven years. It is only about six years ago that the maximum penalty was increased to 14 years which it presently is under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. We are now providing for a maximum penalty of life imprisonment which represents a substantial and real increase in the severity of the penalty. I would ask hon. members to remind themselves that a person convicted and sentenced for trafficking on a second or any subsequent offence will be liable to an indeterminate sentence and in these circumstances he would be released only on the certificate of the parole board and would be under supervision of the parole board for life. In these ways we think, first, we have provided a sufficient increase in the maximum penalty to indicate to the courts, the country as a whole and the traffickers themselves the detestation in which this crime is held and to provide the courts with sufficient means of ordering detention in the case of these offences. If this does not work the first time, an offender [DOT] will be subject to an indeterminate sentence which would have the effect of his being under supervision for life even if he should be released from prison.
On these general grounds, therefore, I am unable to accept the amendment. There is a particular ground, too, with respect to the drafting. It will be observed that clause 4 now provides that every person who violates subsection (1) or (2) is guilty of an indictable 

offence and is liable to imprisonment for life. This relates to all traffickers, whether the trafficking results from personal addiction or whether it falls into the still viler class of trafficking for profit. The penalty can be exacted with respect to both kinds of traffickers. Therefore, the effect of the amendment would be to make all traffickers liable to the death penalty. I appreciate that this is a technical matter, and that it could probably be dealt with. Nevertheless, the effect of the amendment would be as I have indicated- a person who is forced into drug trafficking because he himself is addicted and has no other means of sustaining his drug habit would be liable to the effect of the amendment. Thus, though I appreciate and to some extent accept the sentiments of the mover of the motion I am unable to go all the way with him and accept his amendment.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
I think the minister has confirmed the interpretation which I myself was placing on this amendment, because he has said it was an alternative to life imprisonment. I think that is what should be hanging over the heads of these people who are drug traffickers-the possibility that they may be executed. The minister has clearly drawn to the attention of the committee that this was exactly what I was trying to do. Also, the trafficker who is not a user himself is purely in the business for the sake of the financial reward and I can see no value in attempting the rehabilitation of an individual of this type. He goes into it consciously. I would suggest such an individual causes more hardship and misery than a murderer who kills one person, because in the trafficking of narcotics, as we have seen in the city of Vancouver, he can ruin the lives of approximately 3,000 individuals.
I feel the state should not be obliged to pay approximately $2,000 per year to maintain a person who has been sentenced to life imprisonment for the crime of trafficking. I do not think the state should be required or prepared to go to that expense, as those individuals are involved in this business solely with the motive of profit. I think that has been borne out by the fact that the Mafia decided, after its Appalachian conference, because sentences had been increased and enforcement was becoming stronger, to get out of the business. That is exactly the result which I hope will come from the inclusion of the death penalty. There may never be a case where it has to be carried out but, if we consider it as a deterrent under the Criminal Code in respect of those amendments put forth regarding the crime of murder, surely it

will be more of a deterrent to those individuals in the field of trafficking with the sole motive of making a profit.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the amendments to the Criminal Code dealing with capital punishment were under consideration, I mentioned that traffickers, those who promote the sale of narcotics-not the drug addicts, but the traffickers-should also be liable to the death penalty.
An amendment is being introduced today and, in my opinion, a distinction is in order. There are actually two types of drug traffickers: first, those who are drug addicts themselves and who sell drugs for the leader of a drug ring; and then those who are not addicted but who peddle drugs here and there.
Narcotics are being sold in universities, in colleges, in a word, in all spheres of society.
It has been said that capital punishment applies only to a criminal convicted of capital murder. According to me, the worst murderer is the person who is responsible for drug addiction, who sells drugs to people who will develop the habit which, in time, may become compulsive and possibly make criminals out of the addicts. In fact they are victims. It is the trafficker who is the true culprit, the real murderer. He is the one who prepares murderers through his activities.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I strongly support the proposal made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Drysdale). Indeed, in spite of all the amendments to the law and of the R.C.M.P.'s work throughout the country, the latter cannot always get to the brains of drug traffic rings.
The worst individual is not the one who, having become an addict himself, must peddle drugs to satisfy his own needs, but the individual who has set up vast traffic rings. The latter is fully conscious of what he does. His only concern is to make big profits for himself. In my opinion, that is the worst kind of criminals we have in Canada and capital punishment should be their penalty.
For those reasons, I am in favour of the amendment.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF DISTRIBUTION AND SALE OF NARCOTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with great attention to what the mover of the amendment had to say and to the answer given by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton).
As the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) has just stated, we have before us a bill
Narcotic Drug Control
dealing with what may be the foulest crime society has to cope with.
Many lawyers can see for themselves the pernicious effects narcotics have on an individual.
All means possible should be taken to protect society against traffickers. For the protection of society, capital punishment is imposed on those who commit capital murder. They have to die to pay their debt to society. But who could tell all the murders committed not by the victims of traffickers but by the traffickers themselves, who are, as far as we are concerned, members of the underworld.
These traffickers unfortunately operate on a great scale in many places and especially in Montreal as far as the province of Quebec is concerned.
Youth must be protected. All possible means must be taken to avoid the social disturbances caused by drug users. We must do everything to curb this social evil.
That is why I congratulate the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Drysdale) for his amendment. Nothing must be neglected to give the fullest effect to the legislation we are considering now.
I think all hon. members have the same object in mind: to check this plague and make sure that the penalties will be as severe as can be for those who go about spreading social death around them. By spreading death, I mean that their victims become poor human trash. That is why they are not entitled to any consideration from society since they do not have any for anybody, their only concern being to satisfy their greed.
For those reasons, I will vote for the amendment proposed by the member for Burnaby-Richmond.

The death penalty was introduced there much too recently for us to have any information. I am told that the third one is possibly nationalist China. These are the only countries where the death penalty is, according to our information and our present supposition, provided for the offence of trafficking. I remind the hon. member who probably came in after I had spoken earlier that six years ago the maximum penalty was seven years. At that time it was raised to 14 years. We are now raising it to life imprisonment so that a trafficker can be put away for life. If by any chance he should be released and then recommit his offence he is automatically subject to an indeterminate sentence and to supervision for the rest of his natural life. Therefore it cannot be said the penalty being provided is other than very severe.
Let me emphasize again that as the amendment is drawn it makes no distinction between the trafficker who traffics to support his own craving for drugs and those who are traffickers for profit. Penitentiaries Act PENITENTIARIES

speakerposition: topic

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-105, respecting penitentiaries.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it may be of interest to the house to know the first act of the parliament of Canada in relation to the subject matter of penitentiaries was passed in 1868. From time to time thereafter statutes were enacted by parliament in relation to this subject matter, but it was not until 1883 that all the relevant legislation was gathered together and enacted by parliament as an act to amend and consolidate the laws relating to penitentiaries.
Since 1883 the Penitentiary Act has been amended from time to time in one respect or another but at no time until now has parliament been presented with a bill that would revise completely the Penitentiary Act and put it in a form and give it a substance consistent with an enlightened approach to the problem of penitentiary operations. Evidence of this is to be found in the fact that, of the 82 sections in the present Penitentiary Act, more than 50 repeat almost word for word the corresponding section that was enacted by parliament in the statute of 1883 to which I have referred.
Hon. members will recall that the Fauteux committee, in its report of 1956 concerning the principles and procedures followed in the remission service of the Department of Justice, went into a considerable number of further fields than those encompassed by its terms of reference and embraced, indeed, the whole of the penitentiary system. They pointed out that there are certain features which, in the opinion of the committee, should be emphasized in the development of the Canadian correctional system. The Fauteux committee enumerated those features as follows:
(a)	a high degree of integration between all parts of the correctional system;
(b)	a well developed and extensive system of adult probation;
(e)	a concentration of effort on treatment by way of training, rather than the mere imposition of punishment; this is especially so in the case of special classes of offenders, particularly youthful offenders and persistent offenders;
(d)	specialization of institutions and specialization of methods of treatment, with a concentration of professional staff in the areas where it is most needed;
(e)	the development of small, open, minimum security institutions;
(f)	a planned policy of recruitment and training of professional staff; and
(g)	a willingness to make full-scale experiments in all phases of the correctional system.
Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that on Friday or Saturday of last week I outlined

Penitentiaries Act
to the committee of supply the progress made by the government in implementing the recommendations of the Fauteux committee report as expanded by the correctional planning committee which we appointed at the end of 1958. I indicated at that time that much progress had been made in modernizing the Canadian correctional system and that, in introducing the present bill, I would be introducing a measure to give form and substance and legislative authority, if you like, to the reorganization that has been going on in the penitentiaries branch as a result of the implementation of these plans.
The purpose of the present bill is to provide the legislative authority necessary in order to develop, in the Canadian federal correctional system, those features that relate particularly to the operation of the penitentiaries. The principal changes, therefore, under the new act that hon. members will find, in comparing it with the present Penitentiary Act, are as follows:
1.	It will permit a reorganization of the headquarters of the service in Ottawa along functional lines and will permit the establishment of regional penitentiary directors. This headquarters reorganization and regional development is essential if the headquarters of the service in Ottawa is not to be bogged down by a mass of details concerning the day to day operation of individual institutions.
2.	This bill will bring all officers and employees of the service under one central authority for the purposes of appointment, promotion and transfer. I outlined, during the consideration of the estimates, the new approach to this staff problem, and the new career opportunities which would open up. Prior to 1933 penitentiary officers were appointed under and were subject to the Civil Service Act. Since 1933 the headquarters staff in Ottawa has been appointed by the civil service commission; wardens, deputy wardens and other administrative or executive officers in the institutions have been appointed by the governor in council on the recommendation of the commissioner approved by the minister; and all other employees in penitentiaries, such as guards, trade instructors and other subordinate officers have been appointed by the commissioner upon the recommendation of the warden of the penitentiary concerned.
This is a very unsatisfactory arrangement because it does not permit transfers and promotions of officers between headquarters and the field. If we have a penitentiary officer who is, in our opinion, eminently suitable for a position at headquarters, it is necessary for him to enter a civil service competition and, of course, there is no assurance that he will win it. If he does win the competition,

he must then resign his position on the penitentiary staff in order to accept the new position under the Civil Service Act.
It is essential that all officers and employees should come under one jurisdiction and that the penitentiary service should be organized in a way that will permit, first:
The development of a career service, in which promotions are made on the basis of career planning and specialized training: for example, the headquarters staff should, as far as possible, have had experience in institutional work and the benefit of specialized correctional training.
Second, it is also necessary that the service should be organized in a way that will permit a code of discipline applicable to penitentiary service officers, especially in the field, comparable to that of the R.C.M. Police.
Third, it is necessary to provide for the speedy appointment of institutional staff members, having regard to the responsibility of the penitentiary service to see to the safe custody of inmates committed to the penitentiary by the courts. The method of appointment of employees established by this clause will give much greater flexibility to our system of career planning for officers.
The next feature that hon. members will observe in comparing this bill with the present act is that the bill authorizes the Minister of Justice, with the approval of the governor in council, to enter into an agreement with the government of any province for the confinement in federal institutions of persons who are sentenced under the criminal law to less than two years. In the absence of such authority persons sentenced to less than two years could not be detained in a federal institution.
The house will recall that in 1958 we had a dominion-provincial conference related to prospective changes being made in Canada's correctional system. This conference was called for the purpose of discussing with the responsible provincial ministers the problems that arise in connection with the implementation of the Fauteux committee's recommendations and other recommendations that we had developed as a result of our consideration of that report. At that time it was stated as a matter of policy by the federal government that we were prepared to accept the Fauteux committee's recommendation that the federal system should assume the responsibility for persons sentenced in Canada to terms of more than six months. I think that recommendation was "sentenced to terms of more than one year".
We outlined the problems that would confront us in accepting this proposal and the planning which would be necessary if we were to put it into effect. I refer to planning related to the improvement of our own federal

system in order to bring it to a point where it was of such a standard that we could say that it was as good as or better than any existing provincial system and that therefore it would be logical and proper for us to accept this additional responsibility; and also planning that would be necessary in order to enlarge the facilities of the federal system so that we might be physically able to take over that extra responsibility.
At that time I indicated to the provinces that if they agreed that this approach was correct, we would base our penitentiary planning on the first assumption and would press on with the necessary reorganization as rapidly as possible; but that in view of the tremendous physical problems with which we were confronted under the responsibility that we then had, it would in fact be several years before we could expect to be in a position to take over the increased responsibility consequent upon the inclusion in our institution of prisoners sentenced to the shorter term. I said, however, that although it might be a matter of years, as it will be, before we would be in a position to implement this recommendation in full, nevertheless, in individual cases where a particular province or particular provinces might find that they had a situation in which they were confronted with the necessity of substantial expenditures on their own part in order to modernize perhaps their own prison system and where they were reluctant to undertake this large scale development to the provincial prison system, we might be prepared to enter into individual arrangements with them under which we would assume, by virtue of agreements then to be entered into, the responsibility for prisoners who would otherwise have been part of the provincial system.
This would have two results. First, it would save the province concerned large outlays on their system which they might find it difficult to make and which might in part at least be wasted because, within a matter of a year or two, we would be taking over their system. Second, it would have the result that, by our assumption of this responsibility under these individual agreements, we would be in a position in which we would be able to plan any development of the prison system in that province so that it would conform with our over-all plan for the ultimate overall federal correctional system. I have reference now to this part of our understanding with the provinces, namely, our understanding that we will be prepared, in advance of the over-all acceptance of the additional responsibility, to enter into agreements with individual provinces to solve their problems.
I should emphasize that the purpose of this change to which I have just drawn attention
Penitentiaries Act
in the new bill is not designed to implement in full the understanding reached at the dominion-provincial conference of 1958, but rather is merely an interim measure designed to provide authority under which this basic change in the law can be made on an overall basis. Arrangements may nevertheless be made between the federal government and certain provincial governments whereby inmates who are now the responsibility of the provinces may be detained in federal institutions at provincial expense.
One major change to which I should draw attention will give effect in part to another understanding reached at the dominion-provincial conference of 1958. This was to the effect that no person under the age of 16 should be sentenced to a penal institution where adults are confined except where he is convicted of an offence mentioned in section 413 of the Criminal Code. This section includes such offences as murder, manslaughter, and rape. In order to give full effect to the recommendation to which I have referred, an amendment to the Criminal Code would be necessary. However, such an amendment to the Criminal Code could not reasonably be presented to this house for consideration until the necessary institutions, either federal or provincial, are available for the confinement of persons under the age of 21 years. What this bill does, however, is to provide that where facilities exist for the separate confinement of young offenders within a region of Canada no person who, being under the age of 16 years, and having been sentenced to penitentiary, shall within that region be confined in association with persons who are 21 years of age or more unless the commissioner otherwise directs in writing.
Then again, this bill changes the method whereby an inmate qualifies for remission of his sentence by reason of good conduct and industry while he is in the institution. The relevant factors to be considered in connection with remission of sentence and parole would seem to be the following. First, it should operate as an incentive to the inmate to apply himself towards his self-improvement while he is in the institution. Second, there should be a parole period of reasonable length for those who are granted parole so that they can obtain full benefit from it and be under supervision for a reasonable period. Third, there should be an incentive to the inmate to accept parole when it is offered to him rather than to serve out his sentence to completion. At the present time, by virtue of section 69 of the Penitentiary Act, an inmate earns remission at the rate of six days

Penitentiaries Act
a month until he has accumulated 72 days, whereupon he earns it at the rate of 10 days a month.
This bill is designed to achieve the purposes that should be served by a system of remission by dividing it into two types: statutory remission, amounting to one quarter of the sentence, which will be credited to the inmate as soon as he arrives in the institution and which will not only be subject to forfeiture for disciplinary offences committed while he is in custody but will also constitute part of his parole period, if he is granted parole; and second, earned remission, under which the inmate will be motivated to apply himself industriously to his work, in order that he may shorten his sentence by three days for each month in which he works industriously and provide an added incentive because, having earned this time off by reason of his industry, it will not be taken away from him by way of disciplinary procedure nor will it constitute part of his parole period.
Further, this bill also provides for the remission of forfeited statutory remission in proper cases. Some inmates have difficulty in adjusting to prison life at the beginning of their sentences and, as a result, have remission forfeited for disciplinary reasons. In time, however, many of these inmates become well adjusted and benefit from the prison program. It is desirable that, where such improvement has taken place, authority should exist for the return to the inmate of statutory remission that he may have lost early in the sentence by reason of his failure at that time to adjust to prison life.
Another feature of the bill is that it also authorizes the commissioner or the officer in charge of a penitentiary, in proper cases, to authorize an inmate to be absent from the institution, with or without escort as the case may be, for medical or humanitarian reasons or to assist in the inmate's rehabilitation. Under the law as it exists at the present time an inmate may not be absent from the institution, without escort, except under the authority of His Excellency the Governor General, acting on the advice of a minister of the crown. This is done as an exercise of the prerogative of mercy.
I am quite sure hon. members will appreciate that there are many, many situations in which it becomes cumbersome and administratively unwise to seek the authority of His Excellency the Governor General every time it appears desirable to allow an inmate, for a short period, to be absent from the penitentiary. Therefore it seems to us to be desirable that the authority to authorize such absences should to an appropriate degree be vested in the commissioner or the officer in

charge of the institution in order that it can be exercised as a part of the over-all training program that has been designed for the inmate in the institution.
The eighth major change is that the bill authorizes the establishment of a committee to be called the advisory committee on penitentiary industry in order that the penitentiary administration may have the benefit of the best advice available in connection with the development of industrial training programs designed to fit inmates for employment in industry and free society when they leave the institution.
Finally, the bill provides for the enactment of regulations by the governor in council for the organization, training, discipline, efficiency, administration and good government of the service; for the custody, treatment, training, employment and discipline of inmates and, generally, for carrying into effect the purposes and provisions of this act. These are regulations which, under the present act, the commissioner himself could make subject only to the approval of the minister. The regulations so made will, of course, be subject to tabling in the House of Commons by virtue of the Regulations Act.
As will have been apparent to hon. members in the course of the discussion that attended the passage of the penitentiary service estimates last week, we have embarked upon a program of penitentiary development that is designed to provide for Canada, in the shortest possible time, a penal system that is at least the equal of any in the world. The science of correcting the offender is developing rapidly. This bill is designed to enable the Canadian penitentiary service to take full advantage of that science and to put it to full use on behalf of the people of Canada.

speechtext:
-I have the choice of speaking at some length on second reading or on the resolution. In view of the fact that the resolution calls for the expenditure of public money I think the reasons why

we are asking the House of Commons to amend the section of the act that we have before us should be advanced at this time.
The purpose of this bill is to amend the Farm Credit Act by increasing the authorized capital of the farm credit corporation from $8 million to $12 million. Under the provision of section 13 of this act, this will have the effect of increasing by $100 million the amount which the corporation may borrow from the Minister of Finance. I believe the reasons behind this proposed increase are of sufficient general interest to justify some comment at this stage.
It will be recalled that when the Farm Credit Act was being debated in committee on July 13, 1959, as reported at page 5948 of Hansard, my predecessor found it necessary, in order to refute criticism that the proposed act did not meet the expressed needs of the Canadian agricultural community, to place on record the comment of a leading official of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, to the effect that the new act embodied practically everything which the federation had proposed.
In view of some of the comments made during that debate there seemed then to be, and there may still exist, some question in some quarters whether the expectations of the government and of the Canadian farmers were going to be justified when the Farm Credit Act became operative. I believe that the bill now before us, if examined in the light of its real implications, will reveal whether those expectations have been realized. To understand those implications it is necessary to refer very briefly to the intent of the Farm Credit Act as conceived by the government at the time of its introduction in this house, and to the record of lending operations that followed its implementation.
It will be recalled that the legislation of 1959 had the effect of increasing the amount and broadening the basis of the security requirements of long term mortgage loans to Canadian farmers. The express object was:
-to assist Canadian agriculture to voluntarily reorganize itself into economic family farm units, each of sufficient size to be capable, under the management of the owner, of producing sufficient income to pay operating and maintenance costs, provide a good standard of living, and to repay the loan necessary to set up such a unit within an appropriate period.
While there was general agreement that increased credit facilities were required, there were many who questioned the adequacy of the government's proposals and their reception by the farming community. I would like to reassure these critics by outlining very briefly the circumstances which make the proposed amendment necessary.

It will be conceded that an objective appraisal of the reaction of the farming public to the new Farm Credit Act can be made only by examining the record of lending activity since the establishment of the farm credit corporation and comparing it to the record under the previous legislation. I may say at the outset that it is this record which necessitates the amendment we now have under consideration.
The Canadian farm loan board in 1929, the first year of its operations, loaned $2,630,377 to 1,270 farmers. During the first decade its annual average lending	amounted	to$3,862,725 and the average number of borrowers was 1,889. During the second decade the average annual lending dropped to $2,669,675 and the average number of borrowers was 1,196. In the third and final decade of its operations it averaged $10,358,134 in loans to an average of 2,378 farmers each year. The total amount of all its outstanding loans at the end of its last full year of operations	amounted	to

Yes, that was the total amount of all its outstanding loans. The Farm Credit Act came into force in the fall of 1959 and on March 31 this year the farm credit corporation concluded its first full fiscal year of lending activity. During that year it approved 5,597 loans in the amount of $60,704,050. As of March 31, 1961, the total of its outstanding investment in farm loans had increased to $162,534,854.
While it is true that we are here comparing the long term averages with a rather brief period under the new legislation, it should be borne in mind that the trend in lending volume under the new farm credit corporation has been continuously upwards and may reach $75 million during the current season. These figures in themselves are conclusive evidence of the enthusiasm with which this legislation was greeted by the Canadian farmer, but they tell only part of the story.
The government's object was to try to ensure that the credit extended to farmers would not only allow them to adjust their operations and their living standards to modern conditions, but would also be within their capacity to repay. Our supporting evidence here is their repayment record. As at March 31, 1960, 90.9. per cent of all mortgage loans were in good standing. By March 31, 1961, this percentage had risen to 92,5 per cent despite the increase in the average amount of the individual loan and the correspondingly heavier repayment obligation.

Farm Credit Act
This speaks well of the care exercised by the farm credit corporation in ensuring that its loans are sound and constructive and in line with the intent of the act, and it illustrates the soundness of the new and intensive program of pre-loan counselling service which its staff extends to all loan applicants.
The soundness of the new legislation and of the farmers' reaction to it is also confirmed by an analysis of the purposes for which loans are made. For example, in 195657 only 33.6 per cent was used to purchase land and effect improvements to land; in 1960-61 the proportion used for these purposes was 59.9 per cent, almost double. This means more emphasis on increased income. In 1956-57 54.1 per cent was used to pay existing land debts and other debts; in 196061 the percentage used for this purpose was only 34.7 per cent.
These figures taken together represent and confirm the government's expectation that the Canadian farmer, given access to adequate and well-administered credit, could be depended upon to put it to good and productive use, in line with the state objective of the legislation-"The progressive reorganization of agriculture into economic family farm units."
I should perhaps interject a word at this point about the cost of administering these improved services to farmers. The net administrative cost to the corporation, expressed as a percentage of the outstanding loan investment, amounted to .865 per cent during the fiscal year just ended, down from an average of 1.06 per cent during the previous four years.
The figures I quoted a moment ago illustrate the farmer's investment of this new long term credit in the creative and productive development of the farming unit. This does not mean that his short and intermediate term credit needs have been neglected. In the year ended December 31, 1960, he also took advantage of government guaranteed bank credit under the Farm Improvement Loans Act to the extent of $79,942,352 to purchase agricultural implements; $10,064,430 for farm buildings; $9,624,919 to purchase livestock; and $2,224,045 for other purposes related to the development of his farming enterprise, for a total of $101,855,746 up from a total of just over $69 million in 1957, $70 million in 1956, $69 million in 1957 and $62 million in 1959.
Working together and complementing each other, these two sources-each performing a separate function and serving a different need-make adequate credit available to establish an economic farm unit for every farmer who is able to establish that he has a sound proposition, the necessary managerial

Farm Credit Act
ability, credit-worthiness and the minimum financial resources required. If he has $9,000 in cash or in land, stock and equipment and the other required qualifications, he can borrow up to $27,500 from these two sources, giving him a working capital of $36,500. Should he be a young and beginner farmer- where the early repayment of a farm improvement loan, along with an F.C.C. loan, would be more than he could reasonably handle-he may borrow the whole $27,500 as a "package-deal" loan under Part III of the Farm Credit Act, in which case he will actually pay interest only on his land debt while repaying the part of the debt secured by his stock and equipment. Under this latter arrangement he also has, during the early years of his enterprise, the advantage of a supervision service provided by the corporation. By the use of one or both of these pieces of legislation, full-time farmers who have acquired 25 per cent of the capital required for the setting up of an economic family farm unit can now be adequately serviced. Of these, the only applicant likely to be turned down is one who cannot establish to the satisfaction of the corporation, by his past record and by a sound operating plan, that he will be able to pay operating, maintenance and living costs and at the same time repay the loan requested, or one who already has an adequate economic unit or sufficient capital of his own to complete or acquire such a unit.
The Canadian farmer's response to these two pieces of credit legislation has been extremely gratifying to this government, illustrating as it does not only the soundness of its over-all agricultural policy, but justifying the confidence it has continued to place in the basic soundness of the agricultural industry itself. Wherever the natural conditions are such as to make commercial agriculture feasible and profitable under modem conditions, our farmers have shown us, I think, that they require only a little encouragement and co-operation from the government in order to work out their own salvation. Their response to the farm credit legislation, reflected in the expanding lending operations of the farm credit corporation and of the banks under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, speaks for itself.
To recapitulate the situation with respect to the capital requirements of the corporation: the lending authority of the Minister of Finance, in so far as the farm credit corporation is concerned, is limited by the corporation's present capital to a maximum of $200 million. The corporation to date has on loan from the Minister of Finance a total of $151,653,944, leaving only $48,346,056 to finance new farm loans for the current season. The greater part of this balance is

already encumbered by loans in process, and it is anticipated that loan demand during the current fiscal year may reach $75 million. The proposed amendment would provide an additional $100 million to meet these credit needs.

I had intended, and I think most people on this side of the chamber had intended, to be very brief on the resolution stage, but we usually find that the Minister of Agriculture has something to sell and a great deal to say.
I am sure he has found since he has been in the Department of Agriculture that those who are employed in that department in the most useful way are engaged in trying to grow ten plants where one was formerly grown. But encouraged by the great number of public relations officers who have been added to the staff of the ministry of late, I am sure that the minister is determined always to use ten words where one word was used before. Thus some reply is necessary, I think, even with respect to legislation which normally would have the swift approval of this committee.
If hon. members would look at the resolution they will find it seems to be a very simple one. Some of us might think it involves only $4 million extra capital. It does not mean that, because while it says that the capital of the farm credit corporation is to be allowed to increase from $8 million to $12 million we must recollect, if we have not looked at the statute recently, that there is a multiplication factor here involving an increase of 25 times the capital of the corporation which means that what we are really doing in connection with this simple resolution is saying that the amount which will be available for lending will be increased, not by $4 million but by 25 times $4 million, which is $100 million.
As I have indicated, I had intended, had the minister not been somewhat verbose, to say with some alacrity that we have very little quarrel with that proposal. However, I now feel that while the resolution, on the face of it, appears to be simple it does involve an examination of the entire operation of the farm credit corporation. Let me say, first of all, that in so far as the financial operations of this corporation are concerned we are more than a year out of date. The last financial report available to us, as far as I know, is the public document provided by the corporation to parliament covering its first year of operation, under a new system, for the year ending March 31, 1960. I therefore suggest to the minister, inasmuch as under the new act we are for the first time embarking upon an element of subsidy and

bonuses in connection with farm loans, that he should provide to parliament when he speaks on the introduction of the bill and on second reading, an up to date statement concerning the salient factors of these operations covering the period between March 13, 1960 and March 31, 1961.
1 thank the minister for the figures he has given us today in connection with gross lending and matters of that kind. The minister very properly took pride in connection with the very obvious growth in gross lending and I might say that we too are pleased to see this. On the other hand I thought the minister was not as objective as he might have been in this case because, if he will look at the first reports presented by this government in the year ending March 31, 1959 in respect to farm loans, he will find figures at page 4 indicating that it was not unusual to have prominent growth, year by year, in the dollar value of farm loan lendings either under the former legislation or under this new act.
To illustrate that fact, I should like to point out that from 1956 to 1957 farm loans increased from $8.2 million to $13.2 million, and from 1957 to 1958 they increased from $13.2 million to $19.3 million, and so on over the years. There has been a general increase which I believe has been comparable to the growth in the gross national product as well as to the dollar growth of our industries across Canada during the same period. There has been, to use the phrase of the minister, a continuously upward increase in loans that have been provided to farmers under the former statute and under the present one.
I have no desire to detract at all from the good growth which has developed under the statute introduced in 1959. However, inasmuch as the minister chose, when it was known to him that this legislation could go through very rapidly, to point to certain features of improvement that were provided in 1959, I felt obliged to inform this committee that this farm loan legislation was introduced in 1929, and that there never was anything but an advance in so far as the maximum amount of loan is concerned except during that period of Conservative administration from 1930 to 1935.
In 1929 when the original legislation was provided, the maximum loan was $10,000. That maximum was reduced in 1934, under the Bennett administration, to $7,500, and was further reduced in 1935 to $6,000. Fortunately the trend ever since, either under one administration or the other, has been upward. I should not have mentioned these matters had it not been for the rather lengthy outline given by the minister.

As the hon. member for Timmins expressed it, he is completely in support of it and to use his exact words, it has provided the farmer with a very necessary service. I think we all agree with that.
One of the most important things that has come out of this act is the counselling by those who are administering the legislation. There is no question about it at all, the growth of money which is going into the purchase of agricultural land shows that this act deals with a situation which was becoming chronic in Canada. Many of the farmers' orchards were too small in size. In other words, they did not have the estimated requirements to make a decent living.
One of the things that comes to mind immediately is the fact that in many instances quite a large percentage of the loans made are in excess of that which was actually requested by the farmer or the orchardist. This came about through what I previously termed "counselling". In other words, a farmer or orchardist wishes to borrow money. He first takes his problem up with the farm credit corporation supervisor or appraiser and gets good solid advice. In other words, what has happened in many instances is this. The appraiser said, "Well, I do not believe that you will have an efficient organization which will put you in a better position if you have only so much. What you need to do is to consolidate all the way through, your debts and so forth, and put yourself on a firm financial basis". This was done throughout my area. I might say that originally the response to this act
Farm Credit Act
overloaded the facilities, but my understanding is that it is being run smoothly and efficiently now.
Certainly, great credit is due to those who came from the Veterans' Land Act administration to act as appraisers. They have done a fantastic job. Many of them spent long hours, to my own personal knowledge, in making these appraisals. They worked a great deal longer than many civil servants feel is appropriate. These chaps even used a great deal of their spare time to accommodate other people, and they certainly deserve a great deal of credit.
I should like now to say one or two words with regard to the remarks made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. There is no doubt in my mind that he intended to try to fool the people of Canada by saying that there is no difference between this new farm credit corporation and the old Canadian farm loan board. He cited a number of figures and said, "Look; what is happening here is normal growth." Then he used that magical phrase which is used by all finance department experts, he related this to the gross national product. He referred to the years 1957, 1958 and 1959, and indicated that the amount ran up to between $18 million and $19 million. He said, relating that to the gross national product, that it showed normal growth, and that the Conservative government has not gone any further.
I should like him to take a look at the figures for 1960-61 which show the amount has increased to $60 million, which is a tremendous jump from the previous $19 million. Goodness knows what it is going to be this year. If one can gain an indication from the further amount required under the act, there will be a large increase. Certainly, as a statistician, the hon. member is getting into the class of the hon. member for Essex East. I know that if he looks at the little book he has in front of him which contains figures produced by the department, he will get a great deal of satisfaction from realizing that this government has produced something that the previous government never even thought of. We are having good success with this act and the minister and those who work under him deserve commendation.

speechtext: I just have one brief comment to make. I express my regret that the Canadian government will not do for Canadian fishermen what it is doing for the Canadian farmer, that is to provide direct loans through a federal agency to the fishermen, as this measure does for the farmers.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF FARM CREDIT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, very briefly let me say that the proof of the pudding is in the eating. Some figures came to my desk

Farm Credit Act
the other day with regard to the percentage increase in the loans approved during the period from April 1 to May 15 this year as compared with the same period the year before. The increase is over 800 per cent. As I recall the figures, they were $1,450,000 for this year compared with $140,000 for last year. This is an indication, sir, that this policy is well accepted by Alberta farmers. While the legislation and the administration of it still have some bugs, and probably will have for some years I do feel, as one who at one time appraised for the Canadian farm loan board, that the raised limits are of a tremendous advantage.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River dealt with a specific case, and I should like to call that a specialty case. It is all right to talk about a substantial loan on a small poultry farm, but there is no assurance whatever that the persons making the application, admirable though they may be, will be in that business two years from now. There must be full security in respect of the amount. This is what this act calls for, and this is what is required.
Perhaps the minister will accept one suggestion from me, and that is that the appraisal fee, which has been steeply upgraded, should be returnable in whole or in part in the event of the loan being declined. I do feel that, particularly in the case of younger men and their families, this involves a hardship. I wish he would give some consideration to some kind of an amendment.

speechtext:
I take it the minister is going to deal with some of these questions on second reading. I should have asked him, when speaking earlier, if he would, in connection with the resume of operations between March 31, 1960 and March 31, 1961, report upon the borrowings of the corporation from the government and the rate of interest paid. I think it is obvious that this corporation has had to pay the government, under its tight money policy, as much as 5| per cent according to the last budget figures. In view of the fact we are dealing with $100 million additional, I think we should have a report for the most recent fiscal year.

That It is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act to provide that the two hundred million dollar limit of liability specified in section 21B of the act, now applicable to both contracts of insurance entered into by the corporation under section 21 and instruments guaranteed by the corporation under section 21A, be made applicable solely to contracts of insurance entered into under section 21; and further to provide a separate limit, in the amount of two hundred million dollars, on the liability of importers under outstanding instruments guaranteed by the corporation under section 21A.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIMITS OF LIABILITY UNDER SECTION 21
speechtext:
The Export Credits Insurance Act at present provides a ceiling of $200 million for both export credits insurance under section 21 and export credit financing under section 21A.
Under section 21 in cases where the board of directors of the export credits insurance corporation is of the opinion that a proposed contract of insurance would impose upon the corporation a liability for a term or an amount in excess of that which the corporation would normally undertake, and if in the opinion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce it is in the national interest that the proposed contract of insurance to be entered into, the governor in council may authorize the corporation to issue the insurance policy.
Insurance policies in force today under section 21 total $125 million. As insurers of supplier credits, and in accordance with the Berne union understanding, the maximum period of credit that the corporation will insure is five years after delivery. This principle carries the government's approval.
Under section 21A the government has authority through the corporation to finance export sales of capital goods. It is intended that this financing would be provided only where credit terms extending beyond five years are required. Financing commitments under section 21A today total $58 million. Thus, $183 million is committed out of the $200 million available. This leaves only $17 million available for both additional insurance under section 21 and any long term financing under section 21A.
The bill proposes that $200 million available for both insurance under section 21 and financing under section 21A be allocated solely to insurance, and that an additional $200 million be provided for export financing.

Both export credits insurance and export credit financing are an important part of our drive to get Canadian manufacturers into the export markets of the world. The government for its part is doing everything possible to encourage exporters. We had the export trade promotion conference last December; we have held a number of trade conferences around the country since that time; in a splendid example of co-operation between the government and the banks, the nine Canadian chartered banks have established the Export Finance Corporation of Canada, Ltd., which will make financing readily available to capital goods exporters who have export credits insurance; and finally, in cases where longer terms of credit than five years are required and are justified, the government will provide the necessary financing under the Export Credits Insurance Act.
With these facilities in Canada we are offering Canadian exporters the equivalent of anything available to exporters in any other country. I am more than pleased to have to come to parliament to ask for an increase in the financing authority under section 21A of the Export Credits Insurance Act. This requirement shows that our potential is expanding and that exporters are being given every possible assistance to help them increase export sales, both by minimizing their losses with the protection of export credits insurance, and by helping them quote on large orders for capital equipment by providing financing possibilities.

In 1959 when the provisions contained in section 21A and 21B of the act were added to the legislation the government retained the limit on the power to insure under special circumstances with the approval of the governor in council under section 21 and the added power to guarantee and discount paper under section 21A at $200 million, which was the amount that had formerly been the ceiling on insurance only under section 21. In other words, there was in effect a reduction of the amount of business authorized to be covered.
I recall on that occasion raising the point with the then minister of trade and commerce. Indeed, if hon. members will take the trouble to check Hansard, I think they 90205-6-394
Export Credits Insurance Act would find that there was a bit of a hassle over a procedural point because on that occasion the legislation was not preceded by a resolution. In any event, I am glad to see that the authority for insuring under section 21 is being separated, as to the limit of the money available, from the authority to guarantee and discount paper under section 21A. Indeed, at the time section 21A was enacted in 1959, I had gone so far as to suggest that it might more properly be done under a separate corporation as is the case in the United States. However, the government did not see fit to follow that policy and I have no special criticism to offer of that fact. But it is clear that the authority under the two sections should be kept wholly separate and that the authority for the larger amount of guaranteed paper and the larger amount of insurance under section 21 should be granted.
I wonder whether the minister would mind putting in somewhat categorical form on the second reading of the bill based on this resolution the amount of insurance outstanding at the latest available date under section 13 of the act. The amount outstanding which he gave tonight was under section 21 of the act, that is insurance on contracts approved by the governor in council where it is the opinion of the government that the proposed contracts of insurance will impose upon the corporation a liability for a term or an amount in excess of that which the corporation would normally undertake in relation to any one for which authority was being sought. Then will he give the amount separately under 21A of the paper that has been guaranteed and the amount of any paper that has been purchased under the provisions of section 21A. If he could put those figures on the record at second reading it would be helpful.
I wish to raise briefly one other matter that I had asked the minister to consider when the 1959 legislation was before the house at the committee stage. I refer to the provision for tabling the orders in council passed under the act. The requirement is now contained in section 21B, subparagraph 4 which reads as follows:
All orders in council made under sections 21 and 21A while parliament is in session shall be laid before parliament during such session and, if made while parliament is not in session, shall be laid before parliament at the next ensuing session.
That provision, as will be seen, merely requires the tabling of orders in council passed under the section of the act on the closing day of a session. Indeed on June 9 there was tabled a quite important order in council dated September 16, 1960. The tabling of it at that late date was in full compliance with the law as it exists, but it surely is not a satisfactory procedure. I would hope that the

speechtext:
I think section 23(1) is the particular section to which I am now referring. There will be an amendment of that section.
There are other incidental amendments mainly for the purpose of clarity and simplification of language. At present, section 32 makes no reference to the "rendering of services" and the amendment will make it clear that a certificate is required for this purpose. Similarly the present section 35 makes no reference to "work performed" and the amendment will clearly authorize that payment may be made during the 30 day period following the end of the fiscal year for "work performed".
It is proposed to enact a new subsection to section 95 of the act. This new subsection will permit the comptroller to make recovery of overpayments of salary, wages, pay and pay and allowances from any moneys payable to the person to whom such overpayment is made without the necessity of complying with the procedural requirements of subsection (1) -of section 95. This will result in greater administrative efficiency but will in no way impair the rights of the individual since recovery will only be made with respect to overpayments which it is clear the individual had no right to receive. The comptroller by section 36(3) of the act is presently -empowered to recover any accountable advance or any portion thereof that is not repaid or accounted for out of any moneys payable by Her Majesty to the person to whom the advance was made. The proposed amendment will provide a quick and efficient means of recovering overpayments of salary, wages, pay and pay and allowances in the same manner.
The committee will see that these are all somewhat technical and detailed amendments which I believe it will be simpler to discuss when the bill is before the house.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PURCHASE AND SALE OF SECURITIES BY MINISTER, ETC.
speechtext:
I am sure the committee appreciates the explanation given by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance. I was surprised, having read only the resolution, which is all any of us could read before we reached this stage of the legislation, to find that the parliamentary secretary seemed to emphasize and concentrate upon the fact that we were to get a bill having something to do with a change relative to the assigning of debts, contracts, the forgiveness of debts and so on. I think parliament is entitled to a better explanation of government intentions in a resolution than

we have been given in this one, the parliamentary secretary having told us what he did tonight. This resolution is not a new one and it therefore cannot involve any new idea on the part of the government-any idea it might not have had two months ago. It was given to us on May 29, and there is not a word in it with respect to assignment of debt.
It does refer to three things upon which I was prepared to speak. The parliamentary secretary referred to four points, and one of them, naturally, was something of which members of parliament would have no knowledge until he spoke, because there is no reference to it in this resolution. Of course, we shall wait for the bill.
The first of the three matters with which I am prepared to deal concerns the permission to be granted to the Minister of Finance to buy and sell securities guaranteed by Canada. I know of no securities in that category other than those of the Canadian National Railways. The parliamentary secretary has said it would not be possible for the minister to buy and sell those securities at the present time. He did not say why it has not been possible in the past, nor did he tell us why it is considered advantageous that he should be able to do so in the future. I hope that on second reading we shall have a little more information given us both as to the departmental view on this question of why it was not possible in the past and as to why it would be advantageous in the future.
With respect to what I call the second item, the permission which will be given to the cabinet to delete from the accounts debts not exceeding $1,000. I think this relates, as the parliamentary secretary said, to section 23 of the existing Financial Administration Act. I would expect, inasmuch as nothing has been said to the contrary, that there will be no change in subsection (2) of section 23, and if so I do not think that this proposal will encounter any objection from this side. I refer to what I presume to be the fact that while we are increasing the amount which may be deleted at the instance of the cabinet it would still be subject to a report in the public accounts for the year in question.
